title: feat(acl): a general update task, and a direction for scope filters (#150)
body:
feat(acl): a general update task, and a direction for scope filters (#150)

Two gaps found while folding a maintainer's private acl/* surface onto this
family (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#840 phase A). Neither is
implementation-specific.

## acl/update/0.1

The family could not express "same role, different step-up approver".
`acl/grant` creates and explicitly refuses role changes; `acl/change-role` moves
the role and nothing else; `acl/revoke` removes. A maintainer needing to amend a
label, scope set, expiry, step-up requirement or approve-authority had to model
it as revoke-then-grant — a window in which the subject holds nothing — or
invent a private task.

Two of its refusals are enforced rather than advisory, and both exist so that a
reduction in authority cannot be performed by a task that does not look like
one:

- A role member is rejected (`roleChangeNotPermitted`). `change-role` owns that
  transition because it takes the current role as a compare-and-swap; role is
  the one attribute where a lost update between concurrent writers is a
  privilege change rather than a cosmetic one.
- Narrowing `scopes` is rejected (`narrowingNotPermitted`), directing the caller
  to `acl/revoke`. Removing authority is what an auditor most needs to find and
  it should appear in exactly one place; were narrowing expressible here,
  "withdrew production access" and "corrected a label" would be
  indistinguishable in the trail.

Members replace rather than merge, which keeps *omitted* (leave alone),
*explicit null* (clear) and *empty array* (set to nothing) distinguishable.
A merge cannot tell those apart and cannot express removal at all.

## direction on acl/list

Where scopes are hierarchical, one scope identifier raises two questions: who
may act IN it (entries scoped to it or an ancestor) and what is granted BENEATH
it. `scope` alone answers only the first.

Getting it wrong fails quietly, which is why it is spelled out in the spec: a
revocation sweep using the acting-in reading returns exactly the entries that
are NOT the answer — the ancestors, which keep their authority — while omitting
every leaf-scoped grant underneath. Short rather than empty, so it reads as
complete.

Omitting the member preserves existing behaviour, so this is additive.

## Notes for the next spec author

The `direction` member deliberately carries no JSON Schema `default`. A default
makes codegen emit a non-Option field, so a document omitting the member
deserializes to the default and re-serializes WITH it — breaking the round-trip
conformance test. `default` is annotation-only in JSON Schema anyway; the rule
belongs in prose.

Its schema description is also a single paragraph on purpose. Codegen renders a
multi-paragraph description as indented lines inside `/** */`, which rustdoc
parses as a Rust code block and tries to compile. Reasoning belongs in spec.md,
which is the normative place for it.

CONVENTIONS.md gains a table of which task changes what, plus both enforced
boundaries.

title: feat(acl): a general update task, and a direction for scope filters
body:
Two gaps in the `acl/*` family, both found while folding a maintainer's private ACL surface onto it (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#840 phase A). Neither is implementation-specific — the fold is what surfaced them, not what needs them.

## `acl/update/0.1` — the family cannot currently amend an entry

There is no way to say *"same role, different step-up approver"*. `acl/grant` creates and explicitly refuses role changes; `acl/change-role` moves the role and nothing else; `acl/revoke` removes. A maintainer needing to amend a label, scope set, expiry, step-up requirement or approve-authority had to model it as revoke-then-grant — **a window in which the subject holds nothing** — or invent a private task, which is exactly what happened.

Two refusals in it are enforced rather than advisory, and both exist so a reduction in authority cannot be performed by a task that doesn't look like one:

- **A role member is rejected** (`roleChangeNotPermitted`). `change-role` owns that transition because it takes the current role as a compare-and-swap. Role is the one attribute where a lost update between concurrent writers is a *privilege change* rather than a cosmetic one.
- **Narrowing `scopes` is rejected** (`narrowingNotPermitted`), directing the caller to `acl/revoke`. Removing authority is what an auditor most needs to find, and it should appear in exactly one place. Were narrowing expressible here, "withdrew production access" and "corrected a label" would be indistinguishable in the trail.

Members **replace rather than merge**, which keeps *omitted* (leave alone), *explicit null* (clear) and *empty array* (set to nothing) distinguishable — three intentions a merge cannot tell apart, and under which removal isn't expressible at all.

## `direction` on `acl/list` — one scope, two questions

Where scopes are hierarchical, a scope identifier raises two different questions, and `scope` alone answers only the first:

- **Who may act in this scope?** Entries scoped to it *or to an ancestor* — authority reaches down. (`acting-in`, the behaviour when the member is omitted.)
- **What is granted beneath this scope?** Entries at or below it. (`subtree`.)

It's spelled out in the spec because getting it wrong **fails quietly**: a revocation sweep using the `acting-in` reading returns precisely the entries that are *not* the answer — the ancestors, which keep their authority — while omitting every leaf-scoped grant underneath. Short rather than empty, so it reads as a complete answer.

Additive: omitting the member preserves existing behaviour.

## Two notes for the next spec author

Both cost me a debugging cycle here, so they're in the commit message too:

- **`direction` deliberately carries no JSON Schema `default`.** A default makes codegen emit a non-`Option` field, so a document omitting the member deserializes to the default and re-serializes *with* it — breaking the round-trip conformance test. `default` is annotation-only in JSON Schema anyway; the rule belongs in prose.
- **Its description is one paragraph on purpose.** Codegen renders a multi-paragraph description as indented lines inside `/** */`, which rustdoc parses as a Rust code block and tries to compile — `error: unknown start of token: \``. Reasoning belongs in `spec.md`.

`CONVENTIONS.md` gains a table of which task changes what, plus both enforced boundaries.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 257 specs (256 before), 46 shared schemas
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 303 TS modules
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` — 27 binaries, clean
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate` — clean (invalid-example conformance)
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --doc` — clean
- `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs` / `tsc --noEmit` — clean

title: feat(config)!: fold config and provisioning onto canonical, and stop the VTA rewriting its own DID
body:
First execution step of #840 phase A. Three of the 67 unpublished canonical URIs are gone — folded onto tasks the registry **already publishes**, with **no new specs authored**:

| Was | Now |
|---|---|
| `vta/config/get/1.0` | `config/show/0.1` |
| `vta/config/update/1.0` | `config/patch/0.1` |
| `vta/provision-integration/request/1.0` | `provision/integration/0.2` |

The `spec/vta/` counted exception in `trust_task_manifest.rs` drops **55 → 52**.

`provision-integration` was nearly free: its payload already cited the canonical spec in a doc comment and already dual-accepted the 0.2 camelCase wire form from #517, so the fold was a constant change.

## The VTA could rewrite its own DID at runtime

Found while diffing the payloads, and worth reading on its own.

`config/update` wrote `vta_did` straight into `config.toml` with **no guard at all**, and the write survived a restart. One mistaken call re-pointed the agent's own identity — orphaning every credential it had issued, every ACL grant naming it, and its DID-document linkage.

To be precise about severity: it was super-admin gated (`auth.require_super_admin()`), so this is a **bricking footgun, not a privilege escalation**. Same class as the defect VTC fixed in its P1.1 hardening, where the rationale ports verbatim — a mistaken patch must not strand the daemon auth-dead or re-point the recovery authority.

**The fix rides the fold rather than being bolted on**, because folding onto canonical `config/patch` *required* deciding which keys are patchable. `vta_did` is now a registry key marked immutable: `config/show` returns it, and a patch naming it comes back under `rejected` with a reason.

Two deliberate choices:

- **Immutable rather than absent.** VTC solved its equivalent by leaving `vtc_did` out of the registry entirely. Keeping it *in* and marking it immutable preserves the read path — nothing else exposes the VTA's DID — and answers "identity is set at setup" rather than "unknown key".
- **Enforcement in the registry table, not an `if` in a handler.** One place says what may change and every write path consults it, so a new mutation surface cannot forget the check. `--community-vta-did` is removed from both CLIs: there is no longer a flag to attempt it with.

Pinned by `super_admin_cannot_rewrite_the_vta_identity` end-to-end through the real router, plus four unit tests asserting properties *of the registry table* so a new key cannot quietly become mutable.

## Config is a key registry now, not three named fields

That reshape is what made the fold possible — canonical `config/*` speaks `{key, value, source, requiresRestart}`, and three typed fields could not fold without it. Two things fall out:

- **`public_url` is honestly marked `requiresRestart: true`.** It is read at boot to build the advertised origin, so before this a patch silently diverged the running services from the stored value until someone called `management/reload-services`. Pre-existing; the canonical shape simply has a field for saying so.
- **`config/patch` reports `applied` / `pendingRestart` / `rejected` per key** instead of echoing the whole config, so a caller learns which of its changes actually took effect.

`ConfigResponse` keeps `vta_did()`, `vta_name()` and `public_url()` accessors, so most call sites read as they did before.

## Breaking changes

`GET/PATCH /config` change shape — response is a key registry, patch body is `{overrides: {key: value}}`. `vta_did` is no longer writable through any surface, and `--community-vta-did` is removed from `pnm config update` and `cnm config update`.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --check` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace` clean (as CI runs it)
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk -p vta-service -p vta-cli-common -p pnm-cli -p cnm-cli -p vtc-service`: **88 test binaries, exit 0**, zero failures
- The widened census resolves both new canonical URIs against published `trust_tasks_rs` 0.2.42

title: feat(config)!: fold config and provisioning onto canonical, and stop the VTA rewriting its own DID (#841)
body:
feat(config)!: fold config and provisioning onto canonical, and stop the VTA rewriting its own DID (#841)

* feat(config)!: fold config and provisioning onto canonical, and stop the VTA rewriting its own DID

Three of the 67 unpublished canonical URIs are gone, folded onto tasks the
registry already publishes with no new specs authored:

  vta/config/get/1.0                     -> config/show/0.1
  vta/config/update/1.0                  -> config/patch/0.1
  vta/provision-integration/request/1.0  -> provision/integration/0.2

The `spec/vta/` counted exception in `trust_task_manifest.rs` drops 55 to 52.
`provision-integration` was nearly free: its payload already cited the
canonical spec and already dual-accepted the 0.2 camelCase wire form (#517).

`config/update` wrote `vta_did` straight into `config.toml` with no guard at
all, and the write survived a restart. One mistaken call re-pointed the agent's
own identity, orphaning every credential it had issued, every ACL grant naming
it, and its DID-document linkage.

It was super-admin gated, so a bricking footgun rather than a privilege
escalation — the same class VTC fixed in its P1.1 hardening, and the rationale
ports verbatim: a mistaken patch must not strand the daemon auth-dead or
re-point the recovery authority.

The fix rides the fold rather than being bolted on, because folding onto
canonical `config/patch` REQUIRED deciding which keys are patchable. `vta_did`
is now a registry key marked immutable: `config/show` returns it, and a patch
naming it comes back under `rejected` with a reason.

Immutable rather than absent from the registry (VTC's choice) keeps the read
path — nothing else exposes the VTA's DID — and gives a better answer:
"identity is set at setup" instead of "unknown key".

Enforcement lives in the registry table, not an `if` in a handler: one place
says what may change and every write path consults it, so a new mutation
surface cannot forget the check. `--community-vta-did` is gone from both CLIs;
there is no longer a flag to attempt it with.

That reshape is what made the fold possible — canonical `config/*` speaks
`{key, value, source, requiresRestart}` and three typed fields could not fold
without it. Two things fall out:

- `public_url` is honestly marked `requiresRestart: true`. It is read at boot
  to build the advertised origin, so before this a patch silently diverged the
  running services from the stored value until someone called
  `management/reload-services`.
- `config/patch` reports applied / pendingRestart / rejected per key instead of
  echoing the whole config, so a caller learns which changes took effect.

`ConfigResponse` keeps `vta_did()`, `vta_name()` and `public_url()` accessors
so call sites read as they did before.

BREAKING CHANGE: `GET/PATCH /config` change shape — the response is a key
registry and the patch body is `{overrides: {key: value}}`. `vta_did` is no
longer writable through any surface, and `--community-vta-did` is removed from
`pnm config update` and `cnm config update`.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-support): declare the vti-common feature it actually uses

`seal.rs` calls `KeyspaceHandle::with_encryption`, which is
`#[cfg(feature = "encryption")]` in vti-common. vta-support depended on
vti-common with no features at all.

It built anyway, which is why this went unnoticed: another workspace member
enables `vti-common/encryption`, and cargo's feature unification turns it on
for the whole shared build. `cargo publish` verifies each crate in ISOLATION,
where nothing else is present to enable it — so the method genuinely is not
compiled in, and the tarball fails with E0599.

That is what broke the publish run for vta-support 0.2.0 on main, and it would
have kept failing on every subsequent run: the published vti-common 0.11.28
does carry the method, it was simply never compiled into vta-support's isolated
build. A version bump would not have helped.

Verified with `cargo package -p vta-support`, the same check CI runs. Also swept
every publishable crate the same way; the only other failure is vta-cli-common
against the not-yet-published vta-sdk 0.20.10, which is the ordinary
self-pin transitional state — publish walks crates in dependency order, so
vta-sdk lands before vta-cli-common is attempted.

Worth noting the general shape: a workspace build cannot detect a missing
feature dependency, because unification supplies it from a sibling. Only an
isolated build can, and `cargo package` is the only thing in the pipeline that
does one.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(vta-service): hardened configuration — non-TEE at-rest encryption (#835)
body:
feat(vta-service): hardened configuration — non-TEE at-rest encryption (#835)

* feat: add VTA hardened configuration

Signed-off-by: Yaroslava Kurash <yaroslava.k@affinidi.com>

* fix: offline command store encryption, zeroize CliStore enc_key

Signed-off-by: Yaroslava Kurash <yaroslava.k@affinidi.com>

* feat: bump versions, update changelog, docs

Signed-off-by: Yaroslava Kurash <yaroslava.k@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-service): auto-migrate the store on first hardened boot, and tighten the surrounding edges

Enabling [hardened] on a VTA that already had data made every pre-existing row
unreadable. The store's decrypt path is deliberately fail-closed with no
plaintext fallback — that fallback would reopen the cut-and-paste downgrade hole
the VAE1 AAD binding closes — so the flag could not be a pure config change.
Nothing converted the rows and nothing detected the situation, so the operator
lost access to their own ACL keyspace by flipping one boolean.

migrate_store_to_encrypted runs the conversion at boot before server::run opens
anything, mirroring vtc-service. Idempotent (skips VAE1 rows, so later boots do
one prefix scan and no writes) and crash-safe (an interrupted run is completed by
the next boot). The bootstrap keyspace is excluded: its hardened JWT ciphertext
is read back through a bare handle, so wrapping it in VAE1 would make the next
boot fail as though the ciphertext were tampered with — a test pins that.

Also, from the same review:

- [secrets] seed inlines the master seed in config.toml, which is the one
  backend that defeats this feature outright. It sat on the don't-warn side of
  the plaintext-backend check, so the deployment that most needed the warning
  was the only one that never saw it.
- A missing JWT fingerprint row now self-heals rather than aborting the boot.
  The AES-GCM tag has already authenticated the ciphertext by that point, so
  the fingerprint adds nothing; treating absence as fatal handed a denial of
  service to anyone who could delete a row but not forge a ciphertext, since
  the documented remedy invalidates every session. Mismatch stays fatal.
- load_storage_key_for_cli's Err was collapsed into None at two call sites,
  which opens bare handles against an encrypted store: a secret-store outage
  surfaced as a deserialization error rather than its real cause. The unseal
  path now exits; status prints a note and degrades, since it is a diagnostic.
- vta setup mints a random per-VTA storage_key_salt. Not a fix for a break — an
  HKDF salt need not be secret and the IKM is already a per-VTA seed — but the
  field is documented as a per-VTA constant, so it should be one. Configs
  omitting it keep the legacy constant, so existing stores are unaffected.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(vta-service)!: store the hardened JWT key as an ordinary encrypted row, and fix the didcomm-without-webvh build

Two things, both about removing a footgun rather than adding a feature.

The JWT signing key was sealed with a bespoke AES-GCM blob and parked in the
*unencrypted* bootstrap keyspace, alongside a SHA-256 fingerprint row that
existed to detect tampering with it. That is two encryption schemes where one
would do, and the bespoke one was the weaker: its ciphertext carried no
associated data, so a row copied to another key would still have opened. It now
lives in the encrypted KEYS keyspace at hardened:jwt_key as a plain VAE1 row —
same layer as every other secret, AEAD-bound to its (keyspace, key) location.
The fingerprint row goes with it; the AEAD tag does that job, and a mismatched
salt or seed now surfaces as a decrypt failure on read. A test pins the AAD
binding by relocating an envelope and asserting it no longer opens.

Existing deployments migrate on the next boot: the legacy sealed row is opened,
rewritten into KEYS, and both legacy rows deleted, carrying the key across
unchanged so live sessions survive. load_boot_secrets now owns the ordering,
because the key lives behind an encrypted handle and reading it before
migrate_store_to_encrypted would fail on the first unconverted row.

Separately, cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features
rest,didcomm did not build, on main and before this branch. Three trust-task
call sites buffer into AppState::mediator_registry, which is webvh-gated, from
inside didcomm-gated blocks — naming PendingResponse needs only didcomm, so
nothing failed until the pair was built alone. Every other reference in the
crate is webvh-gated; these were the outliers. Gated them, and left the
Guaranteed sends beside them on didcomm, since those are the delivery path and
the registry buffer is a latency optimisation.

CI never covered that combination because the tee step pulls webvh in, so it
would have regressed again. Added a step that builds it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-service): gate the didcomm-only imports out of the rest-only build

cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest compiled with
six warnings: vta_sdk::acl_setup and two std::time::Duration imports, the
flush_queues parameter, CONSENT_PUSH_DELIVER_BY_SECS and TASK_CONSENT_GRANTED_0_1.

Every one traces to a consumer behind #[cfg(feature = "didcomm")], so each is
gated to match rather than blanket-allowed. flush_queues is the exception and
stays in the signature — callers pass it unconditionally — with a scoped
allow(unused_variables) and a note that a REST-only build has no queues.

Added the combination to CI as a clippy -D warnings step, alongside the
didcomm-without-webvh one. Nothing built either, which is why both rotted.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vta-service): make the seed-on-disk warnings say what is actually lost

Both warnings described the weakness accurately but understated it — "reduces
hardened configuration to obfuscation" reads as a downgrade rather than as
"this provides no protection".

They now carry the SECURITY: prefix the neighbouring env-var warning already
uses, and state the capability directly: anyone who can read the seed
re-derives the storage-encryption key and the JWT signing key, which is enough
to decrypt the whole store and forge any token.

Still warnings, not a refusal: config.toml can legitimately be mounted from a
Kubernetes Secret, where the seed is not on a disk an attacker reaches. The
docs now say that is the reason, so an operator can tell whether the warning
applies to them.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(vta-service): hardened configuration — non-TEE at-rest encryption
body:
## Hardened configuration — non-TEE at-rest encryption

Adds `[hardened] enabled = true` in `config.toml` to bring storage encryption and sealed JWT key management to self-hosted (non-TEE) VTAs — the same protection as TEE layer 3, with the `[secrets]` backend as the trust anchor instead of the Nitro KMS.

### What changes

**Storage encryption** — all fjall keyspaces encrypted with AES-256-GCM (VAE1, same format as TEE). Key is HKDF-SHA256-derived from the master seed on every boot; never written to disk.

**Sealed JWT signing key** — random 32-byte key generated at first boot, AES-GCM sealed under the storage key in the `bootstrap` keyspace, SHA-256 fingerprint-verified on subsequent boots. Boot aborts on mismatch (tamper detection). `vta hardened rotate-jwt` clears it for rotation.

**Offline CLI** — all `vta` offline subcommands (`acl`, `keys`, `vault`, `webvh`, `bootstrap`, `unseal`, …) transparently derive and apply the storage key via the new `CliStore` wrapper.

**Memory safety** — `HardenedBootSecrets` holds `storage_key` and `jwt_key` and zeroizes both on drop, mirroring `tee::kms_bootstrap::BootstrappedSecrets`. `CliStore.enc_key` is also zeroized on drop.

### Crate versions

| Crate | Version | Change |
|---|---|---|
| vta-sdk | 0.20.7 → **0.20.8** | `BackupPayload` / `ImportedSecretBackup` `Drop` impls |
| vta-support | 0.1.x → **0.2.0** | `require_unsealed` signature change; `run_unseal_challenge` + friends gain `enc_key` param |
| vta-service | 0.12.x → **0.13.0** | Hardened configuration feature |
| vta-enclave | → **0.7.7** | Warn + ignore `hardened.enabled` (TEE KMS takes precedence); dep pin update |
| vta-backup, vta-tee | patch bump | vta-support dep pin update |

### Docs updated

- non-interactive-setup.md — canonical operator reference (`#hardened-configuration`)
- tee-architecture.md — mutual exclusivity with TEE
- security-model.md — layer notes
- secret-backends.md — backend selection callout

title: feat(acl): AclEntry gains the approve-vs-act authority axis
body:
Adds `AclEntry.approve` — `{ all?: boolean, scopes?: string[] }` — on the shared `acl/_shared/0.1/acl-entry` component, so all six `acl/*` specs gain it at once.

## What it models

`scopes` says what a subject may **exercise itself**. `approve` says what it may **confer on others** by ratifying an approval — a step-up ratification, a task-consent delegation.

The two axes are independent in both directions, and that independence is the whole point: it is what lets a maintainer configure a **least-privilege approver** — a party that can authorize an operation in a scope it has no authority to perform. A single list cannot express that, which is why this is a new member rather than a widening of `scopes`.

## Why a first-class member and not `ext`

Because the failure direction has to be safe. An absent `approve`, an absent `all`, and an empty `scopes` all mean "may ratify nothing" — so a consumer that hasn't implemented the member confers **less** than the producer intended.

`ext` is explicitly ignorable by design. For an *authority* member that would mean silently dropping a restriction the producer relied on, which inverts the safe direction.

## Consumer rules, now in CONVENTIONS.md

Both have been got wrong in real implementations, so they're stated normatively rather than left to inference:

- **Approve-authority is not authority to act.** Answering "may this party do X" against `approve` hands an approver the ability to perform what it was only meant to sign off on.
- **Emptiness is never a wildcard.** An empty `scopes` or `approve.scopes` means "nothing". The wildcard is `approve.all`, and there is deliberately no `scopes` equivalent — unrestricted authority is expressed through a *role*, not an absent scope list. Reading emptiness as unrestricted is a known privilege-escalation source.

A third section records that granting `approve` is itself an escalation vector — a subject able to grant approve-authority can manufacture an approver for an operation it could not authorize — so maintainers SHOULD gate and audit it more strictly than an ordinary role grant.

## Downstream note

Additive in JSON, but a new struct field **breaks Rust literal construction** of the generated `AclEntry`. The eight in-tree constructors are updated here; downstream consumers need the same one-line addition. Flagging it because "additive schema change" and "additive Rust change" aren't the same thing.

## Why now

Unblocks folding `vta/acl/{create,get,list,update,delete}/1.0` onto canonical `acl/*` (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#840, phase A). Canonical `AclEntry` already covered `subject`, `role`, `label`, `scopes`, `stepUp` and `expiresAt`; the approve axis was the single member with no canonical home, and it's a genuine modelling gap rather than a VTA quirk.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 256 specs, 46 shared schemas
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt --all` — no drift; the change propagates to all six `acl/*` generated types from the one shared component
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 302 TS modules
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` — 27 test binaries, clean
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate` — clean
- `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean
- `tsc --noEmit` — clean

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.42, `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.2.42.

title: docs: reduce-then-author plan for the last 67 unpublished Trust Tasks
body:
Follow-up to #821. **No code changes** — this is the plan for clearing the 67 unpublished canonical URIs the widened census found, which are currently held by counted family exceptions in `trust_task_manifest.rs`.

## The framing

The goal is not "publish 67 specs". A Trust Task is a contract, and publishing 67 where 30 would do is 37 contracts to maintain, version and keep consistent forever. So the order is **fold what already exists, generalise what nearly exists, author only what genuinely doesn't**.

Worth stating up front because it changes the urgency: **these already dispatch over DIDComm and TSP today**. `vta-service`'s trust-task spine routes every one. What's missing is *publication* — the specs are unresolvable, so third parties can't build against them and no consumer can validate a payload it receives. Interoperability and governance gap, not a transport gap.

## Headline findings

**The ACL fold is closer than expected.** Canonical `AclEntry` already carries `subject`, `role`, `label`, `scopes`, `stepUp`, `expiresAt` and the audit members — so five `vta/acl/*` tasks fold with only a payload reconciliation, the one VTC already performed in #710 phase 2d. The single gap is the approve-vs-act axis (`approveAllContexts` / `approveContexts`), and that's a genuine modelling gap in canonical `AclEntry` rather than a VTA quirk: "may confer access but not exercise it" is a generic delegation concept. I'd extend `AclEntry` rather than hide it in `ext` — a consumer that ignores an unknown member then grants *less* than intended, which is the safe direction.

**`did-management/*` and `vta/webvh/*` are two ends of one wire, not duplicates.** The former is what a hosting server implements; the latter what a VTA client does. But for several verbs the payload is the same object crossing two hops — operator→VTA, then VTA→host — where the right answer is *one task dispatched twice*. That's the strongest form of reuse on the table, and needs payload diffs to confirm.

**The twelve vault-lifecycle tasks are two parallel surfaces over two stores** with identical verbs. Publishing all twelve enshrines that duplication; a store discriminator makes it four.

## Estimated outcome

| | Tasks |
|---|---:|
| Bound and unpublished today | 67 |
| Fold onto already-published (A) | −9 |
| Best case from the webvh decision (B) | −8 |
| Vault store discriminator (C) | −8 |
| **Estimated published outcome** | **~42** |

Plus `acl` and `vault` extended, and `vtc/backup/*` folding onto a new generic `backup/*` later.

## Open questions the note flags rather than assumes

- **Vault authorization.** #540 gave the credential store its own `CredentialWrite` capability because removing someone's credentials is higher-trust than removing a password. A single task with a store selector must not let a `VaultWrite` holder reach the credential store by flipping a field. This blocks phase C.
- **Two "needs a diff" rows**: `vta/discovery/capabilities` vs `trust-task-discovery/*`, and `vta/management/reload-services` vs `config/reload`.

## The trap this analysis had to avoid

Recorded from #710, where it cost real time: **names and one-line summaries are not evidence of duplication.** Every fold in the note is either payload-diffed or explicitly marked as needing one.

title: feat(credential-exchange)!: bind published URIs, and guard the whole spec authority (#821)
body:
Closes #821.

The eight `credential-exchange` Trust Tasks now bind URIs the registry actually publishes — `trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.41, authored in [trust-tasks-tf#148](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/148).

Five of them previously existed **only** as files in this repo while claiming a `trusttasks.org` ID no consumer could resolve. The other three — `pending-list`, `pending-approve`, `pending-deny` — had no spec anywhere at all.

## Breaking wire changes on all eight

- Renumbered `1.0` → `0.1`, matching how the rest of the registry versions.
- The operator surface is nested as `pending/{list,approve,deny}` rather than flat siblings of the protocol tasks. The family now reads as what it is: a party-to-party wire protocol, plus an operator surface over the consent backlog it generates.
- **`PendingPresentationSummary` and `RequestedCredentialSummary` serialize camelCase** — `verifier_did` → `verifierDid`, `created_at` → `createdAt`, `credential_query_id` → `credentialQueryId`. Every member of those two is ours, so the registry's casing convention applies.

Two things deliberately *not* changed, because they look like the same class and aren't:

- The **OID4VCI / OID4VP bodies keep snake_case**. `credential_offer`, `dcql_query`, `vp_token` are those specifications' own field names. Renaming them would be wrong, not consistent.
- The **stored deferral record keeps snake_case**. It is fjall-persisted internal state, not a wire type; renaming it would need a data migration for no benefit. The test fixture that builds one stays as it was, which is why only the response assertions moved.

No external consumers of these constants exist, so the rename is free. `trust-tasks/credential-exchange/` is deleted — the specs live upstream now, and a second copy is how the two drift.

## The guard that should have caught this

`every_bound_vtc_task_exists_in_the_registry` only ever checked the `spec/vtc/` prefix. That is precisely why eight URIs on the same authority went unverified for as long as they did.

It is now `every_bound_canonical_task_exists_in_the_registry` and checks **every** `https://trusttasks.org/spec/` URI the workspace binds. A per-family prefix is the wrong shape for the assertion: it defends the family someone remembered to name and silently exempts the next one. The claim being tested is about the *authority* — binding a `trusttasks.org/spec/` URI asserts the registry serves it.

Widening it required separating task URIs from other strings sharing the prefix, done by shape: a Type URI ends in a `MAJOR.MINOR` segment (SPEC §6.1). One rule, two classes excluded — family prefixes used to build or assert URIs (`vta-sdk`'s `ALLOWED_PREFIXES`), and shared-schema `$id`s, which are components rather than tasks.

## It immediately found 67 more

All pre-existing. **None introduced by this PR**, and none a runtime defect — the bindings work, they just reference specs no consumer can fetch.

| Family | Unpublished | What |
|---|---:|---|
| `spec/vta/` | 55 | The bulk of the VTA's own Trust Task surface at `1.0` — keys, contexts, backup, seeds, acl, audit, attestation, config, discovery, management, provision-integration, webvh dids/servers/agent-name. The registry publishes 22 `vta/*` tasks; the workspace binds 77. |
| `spec/vault/` | 12 | The vault + credential-store archival lifecycle (#540), authored as local "openvtc 0.1 extensions" and never taken upstream. |

Plus `spec/trust-task-error/0.1`, which is a permanent and legitimate exception — the framework's error *envelope* is a response type, deliberately absent from the task index.

These are recorded in `UNPUBLISHED_CANONICAL_OK` as family-level exceptions **with asserted counts**. Listing 68 URIs individually would be unreadable; excluding a family without a count would let the next unpublished task in it pass unnoticed, which is the failure the assertion exists to prevent. Pinning the number means the debt can only shrink — publish some upstream and the count drops, add a new unpublished one and the test fails with a message saying which direction it moved and why raising the number is the wrong fix.

I'd suggest tracking the `vta/*` and `vault/*` rows as their own issue rather than folding them in here; they are a much larger piece of work than #821 was, and the same decision (author upstream vs. move to an authority we control) has to be made per family.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --check` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace` clean (as CI runs it)
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk -p vta-service -p vtc-service -p vti-common`: 88 test binaries, exit 0, zero failures (built with the admin UI)
- The widened census resolves all eight new URIs against the published `trust_tasks_rs` 0.2.41 rather than a hand-maintained list

`vta-sdk` 0.20.8, `vta-service` 0.12.43, `vtc-service` 0.11.37.

title: credential-exchange Trust Tasks: specs live only in this repo, and three bound URIs have no spec at all
body:
Split out of #709, which listed `trust-tasks/credential-exchange/{issue,offer,present,query,request}/1.0` as directories "in neither the manifest nor any binding — decide whether those are published or deleted".

Half of that premise no longer holds, and what remains is a different problem.

## Current state

The five directories carry **conformant public-registry IDs** and are **bound live**:

```
https://trusttasks.org/spec/credential-exchange/{issue,offer,present,query,request}/1.0
```

bound by `vta_sdk::protocols::credential_exchange` and dispatched by `vtc-service`. They are absent from `trust-tasks/index.json` **correctly** — that manifest is scoped `org: openvtc, domain: vtc`, and these are cross-domain canonical slugs. Deleting them would delete the only copy of a live wire contract.

## The two real gaps

**1. They are not in the upstream registry.** `trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.39 publishes no `spec/credential-exchange/*` slug — checked against `schema_index.rs` and `src/specs/`. So the specs exist as files in this repo and nowhere a consumer can resolve them, despite claiming a `trusttasks.org` ID. That is the same authority-claim problem #710 fixed for `spec/vtc/*`, one family later.

**2. Three bound URIs have no spec on disk at all:**

```
https://trusttasks.org/spec/credential-exchange/pending-list/1.0
https://trusttasks.org/spec/credential-exchange/pending-approve/1.0
https://trusttasks.org/spec/credential-exchange/pending-deny/1.0
```

`vta-sdk/src/protocols/credential_exchange.rs` defines `PENDING_LIST` / `PENDING_APPROVE` / `PENDING_DENY`, but `trust-tasks/credential-exchange/` has only the five `{issue,offer,present,query,request}` directories. No spec, no schema, not in any manifest.

## Why nothing catches this

`every_bound_vtc_task_exists_in_the_registry` only scans the `spec/vtc/` prefix. `spec/credential-exchange/` bindings pass through every census test untouched — which is how three specless URIs went unnoticed.

## Work

- Author the five existing specs upstream in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, or move them to an authority OpenVTC controls (SPEC 6.5 — the `trusttasks.org` domain is reserved for registry-published specs, the exact rule #710 turned on).
- Author the three `pending-*` specs, or retire the constants if the surface is not meant to be a published Trust Task.
- Widen the census guard so `spec/credential-exchange/*` is checked the way `spec/vtc/*` is, rather than being invisible to it.

Not urgent — this is a published-authority-claim and coverage gap, not a runtime defect. The bindings work; they just reference specs no consumer can fetch.

title: feat: run the join ceremony over TSP when the community offers it
body:
Completes #185 item 2f — the VTC-facing ceremonies can now use TSP.

Both halves land together by necessity: the VTC never initiates TSP to a member (`tsp-enablement.md` §14 Q4), so inbound routing alone would be dead code and outbound alone would throw away the reply.

## Inbound was never a missing transport — only missing routing

`DidCommTransport` owns the one mediator socket and **already** surfaces TSP frames off it, unpacked and sender-authenticated, tagged `Protocol::TSP`. The dispatcher discarded them at its first line — a deliberate placeholder left for this issue. `tsp_frame_to_message` now normalises a frame into the `Message` shape everything downstream already speaks.

That mapping is *lossless* because both transports carry the **same document**. DIDComm's envelope merely repeats two of its members outside it:

| `Message` field | taken from |
|---|---|
| `typ` | the document's `type` |
| `thid` | the document's `threadId` |
| `body` | the whole document — exactly what `tt_didcomm_reply` sets |
| `from` | the TSP-authenticated sender VID, never the document's `issuer` |

So every existing handler works unchanged. **This only holds because #200 landed first** — before it taught the handlers to unwrap `payload`, every TSP reply would have parsed at the wrong nesting and been dropped as malformed.

## Outbound is the one call `pack_and_send` cannot make

It forwards a DIDComm `routing/2.0` envelope unconditionally. `tsp::send_trust_task` is its counterpart with the same signature shape: `send_routed` with the peer's **advertised** mediator as the routing hop and the peer as the final recipient.

## Correlation had to be *made* to agree

DIDComm threads the reply on the request **message** id; TSP has no message and threads on the request **document** id. Two different UUIDs — so the DIDComm message is now built with `id` equal to the document id. `Uuid::parse_str` accepts the `urn:uuid:` form, so the existing correlation code reads either unchanged and one handle works on both wires.

## Discovery degrades quietly

`peer_tsp_mediator` runs the same `#tsp` lookup against the community's document that the VTA path already runs. Not-advertised, unresolvable and timed-out all mean *use DIDComm*, with the distinction kept in the log rather than the return type (R6.4) — there is no panel here to render it into. A community that has not been flipped is unaffected.

## What this deliberately is *not*

An earlier draft registered TSP as a `MessageTransport` on the delivery layer, per the plan in my scoping comment above. That was the wrong fit: the ceremony sends don't go through that layer at all (`pack_and_send` posts straight through the ATM), so an outbox-backed TSP leg would have given TSP joins durability that DIDComm joins lack, and would have meant threading a `Messaging` handle into `join_flow.rs`. Putting the ceremonies behind the outbox is worth doing — for **both** transports, as its own change, rather than hiding a reliability change inside a transport change.

## Verification

Against the live deployment's actual shapes: the test VTC (`did:webvh:QmXi1PZD4…:webvh.storm.ws:first-vtc`) now advertises `#tsp` at the shared mediator, and the VTC accepts Trust Tasks over TSP as of VTI #833, with the member verbs added in #838.

- `cargo test --workspace` — 290 `openvtc-core` + 255 `openvtc` + every integration binary, 0 failed
- Six new tests cover the normaliser, including that a frame with **no proven sender does not inherit the document's `issuer`** — which would otherwise let any TSP peer claim to be the VTC
- `fmt`, `clippy --workspace --all-targets`, `rustdoc -D warnings`, `cargo check --workspace --locked` — all clean

## Follow-ups, not in scope here

- `submit_self_remove` and `send_member_vmc` still send bare bodies over DIDComm. VTI #838 added their Trust Task handlers, but #839 established the document form is reachable over TSP/REST only — so moving them is a wire change *and* a transport change together, worth its own PR.
- Ceremony sends bypass the durable outbox on both transports.

Closes #185

title: TSP: the VTC-facing ceremonies still cannot use TSP (the VTA surface now can)
body:
OpenVTC cannot speak TSP, and until #187 it did not even *say* that a VTA offers it.

Against a TSP-enabled VTA
(`did:webvh:QmWoJD2kpP6AJknNtj7UFERUstEen258ywj3ruHoh1ZAqr:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta`),
whose DID document advertises `#tsp` / `TSPTransport` alongside `#vta-didcomm`,
the VTA panel rendered:

```
Transport:  DIDComm  (in use)   ·   only transport offered
```

which was false — TSP is offered.

## 1. Tell the truth about TSP — **DONE** (#187)

`AdvertisedTransports` gained `tsp_mediator_did`, carried from
`ResolvedVta` (vta-sdk 0.20, upstream #765). The panel now renders
`DIDComm (in use) · TSP advertised (not yet supported)`, keeping
advertised-but-unsupported distinct from both "available" and "absent" (R6.4).
The adjacent `REST endpoint …` inconsistency is fixed too — it is labelled
`(configured; not advertised)` only when the probe positively established the
VTA advertises no `#vta-rest`.

## 2. Speak TSP — **re-scoped**

The upstream blockers (#765, #766, #767) are all closed, and vta-sdk 0.20 ships
`VtaClient::connect_tsp` / `Transport::Tsp`. But the original plan for this
section assumed TSP is a drop-in replacement transport, and it is not. What
follows replaces it.

### What the investigation found

**(a) TSP carries the Trust-Task surface only.** `Transport::Tsp` serves
`rpc_tt`. The VTA's TSP inbound dispatcher hands each unpacked payload to
`dispatch_trust_task_core` and has no handler behind the older DIDComm
*protocol-message* surface, so those operations return `UnsupportedTransport`
**by design** (`vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs:161`, and the `Transport::Tsp` doc at
`:53`).

**(b) Every `VtaClient` operation OpenVTC uses is on the surface TSP does not
carry.** Checked one by one — all `rpc` / `rpc_void`:

| Operation | Call sites | Dispatch |
|---|---|---|
| `get_key_secret` | 13 | `rpc` |
| `create_key` | 7 | `rpc` |
| `create_did_webvh` | 1 | `rpc` |
| `delete_did_webvh` | 1 | `rpc_void` |
| `list_contexts` | 1 | `rpc` |
| `list_webvh_servers` | 1 | `rpc` |

So putting OpenVTC's runtime VTA client on TSP would break key management, DID
minting, and context listing. **This is what invalidates "`build_runtime_vta_client`
becomes a three-way choice" and "add a `VtaTransport::Tsp` variant"** — there is
no single client-wide transport choice that is correct.

**(c) One `VtaClient` surface *can* move today.** `dispatch_trust_task`
implements all three transports (`client/mod.rs:960`), TSP included — same
request/reply document on every one. OpenVTC reaches it from
`agent_name_manage.rs` for the six `did-management/agent-name` Trust Tasks
(set / remove / enable / disable / list / check). That is the whole of the
currently-movable VTA surface.

**(d) The SDK's TSP selection machinery is not on the path OpenVTC uses.**
`TransportChoice` (with `Auto` = TSP > DIDComm > REST, bounded connects via
`TSP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` / `DIDCOMM_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT`, env overrides,
and a deliberately *loud* fallback) lives on
`SessionStore::connect_with_transport` — the `pnm`/`cnm` connect path. OpenVTC
goes through `build_runtime_vta_client` → `VtaClient::connect_auto`, which in
0.20 is still strictly DIDComm-vs-REST with no TSP arm. Either we adopt the
session-store path or we reimplement that policy; **we must not reimplement it
silently**, because the fallback-loudness rationale is the kind of decision the
SDK docs record precisely so consumers don't quietly diverge.

**(e) The messaging layer already supports TSP properly, and this is the bigger
prize.** `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` 0.3.20 — the version already in
our lockfile — has `Protocols { didcomm, tsp }` with `Protocols::BOTH`
multiplexing **both protocols on one websocket per DID** (the mediator allows
only one socket per DID), plus a `TspHandler` trait symmetric with
`DIDCommHandler` and a `TspResponse` the service seals and routes for you. So
per-surface routing at the messaging layer needs **no second mediator session** —
which sidesteps the session-duel and leak hazards this codebase documents at
length. Correlation is explicitly the application's concern: a TSP frame carries
no thread id, so a request/response id has to live in the payload (e.g. a Trust
Task `#response` document's `threadId`).

**(f) The `tsp` feature is cheap.** Enabling it on `vta-sdk` (pulling
`affinidi-tdk/tsp` + `affinidi-messaging-sdk/tsp`) builds clean and costs
**+148,944 bytes on the release binary — +0.82%** (18,112,368 → 18,261,312,
macOS arm64, `lto = true`, `strip = "symbols"`). No reason to make it
conditional.

### Revised work

**2a — Per-surface transport model.** `VtaTransports::in_use` stops being a
single value. A process can be on DIDComm for protocol messages *and* TSP for
trust tasks at the same time, so the panel headline expresses a pair, not a third
enum case. Must stay derivable synchronously from stored config with no network —
the property that lets the panel distinguish "we are on X" from "we could not
ask".

**2b — TSP for the trust-task surface (`dispatch_trust_task`).** Enable the
`tsp` feature; connect TSP *alongside* the DIDComm client rather than instead of
it; route the six `agent_name_manage` operations over it when the VTA advertises
`#tsp`. Protocol-message operations stay on DIDComm — unconditionally, not as a
fallback.

**2c — Transport preference + override.** Persist the operator's choice and
expose an override, so a broken TSP deployment has a documented recovery path to
DIDComm rather than a hang. Mirror `TransportChoice`'s semantics rather than
inventing new ones, including that `Auto`'s fallback is *loud*.

**2d — Bounds and error text.** Every TSP connect and wait bounded (R1.2), with
network-unreachable / not-advertised / auth-rejected carrying distinct text
(R6.4). Reuse the SDK's env-override names where they apply.

**2e — MockVta coverage.** A TSP-advertising VTA in the harness, so the selection
logic has a test that does not need the live deployment.

**2f — Messaging-layer TSP (separate slice, largest).** `Protocols::BOTH` on the
persona listeners plus a `TspHandler` feeding the existing dispatch, for the
VTC-facing ceremonies (join, VIC, credential flows). Blocked on the VTC
advertising `#tsp` and on a correlation decision per (e). Worth its own issue
once 2a–2e land.

## Context

The TSP transport itself is live end-to-end — mediator on
`affinidi-messaging-mediator` 0.17.7, correlated ping, real pongs from the
deployed VTA (#749, #750). The gap was never the wire; it is which surfaces a
client may legitimately move onto it.

title: chore(tee): one home for the TEE store keys, and a changelog guard that can fail
body:
Three small cross-cutting fixes that surfaced while reviewing the TEE / Nitro batch (#819, #824, #826, #827, #832). None of them belongs to any one of those PRs, so they are collected here rather than bolted onto whichever happened to touch the file.

Independent of each other and of the PRs that surfaced them — mergeable in any order.

## 1. `tee:did_log` / `tee:vta_did` get one home

The DID-log store key was a bare string literal in **four** places across three crates:

| Site | Role |
|---|---|
| `vta-tee/src/did_autogen.rs` (×2) | writes it to the `KEYS` (encrypted) and `BOOTSTRAP` (plain) keyspaces |
| `vta-service/src/routes/attestation.rs` | reads it to serve `GET /attestation/did-log` |
| `deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy/src/storage.rs` (×2) | parent-side reader that writes `did.jsonl` to disk |

Renaming the key would have broken the attestation route silently — nothing links the writer to the reader.

`vta_tee::did_autogen` now exports `DID_LOG_STORE_KEY` and `VTA_DID_STORE_KEY`, and every in-workspace reader takes the constant. `enclave-proxy` deliberately **cannot**: it is a separate cargo project running on the *parent* and does not link enclave code. It keeps the literal, now with a comment naming the canonical definition — an honest cross-reference rather than a fake abstraction.

Note for #827: `vta-service/src/tee_webvh.rs` introduces a fifth copy, with a doc comment justifying it as "so this bridge doesn't pull `vta-tee` into `vta-service`'s dependency graph". That rationale doesn't hold — the module is `#[cfg(feature = "tee")]` and `lib.rs` already does `pub use vta_tee as tee;` under the same feature. Whichever of these lands second should use the constant.

## 2. `parent-proxy.sh` bound the DID resolver to the IMDS port

It defaulted `VSOCK_RESOLVER_PORT` to **5400**. On the enclave side 5400 is the IMDS credential proxy and the resolver is **5600** — see `enclave-entrypoint.sh:39-40` and `enclave-proxy/src/main.rs:54,62`. A VTA brought up with this script would have had its resolver leg wired into the credential channel.

The script is also socat-only and covers four of the seven vsock channels — no storage proxy (5500), no log forwarding (5700) — so a VTA deployed with it has no persistent store and no enclave logs on the parent. The header now says that plainly and points at the Rust `enclave-proxy` as the canonical parent implementation, so nobody reaches for the socat path for a real deployment.

Surfaced by #832, which documents all seven channels correctly.

## 3. `check-changelogs.sh` could not fail the case it was written for

The guard matched the version **string anywhere in the file**, not a `<crate> <version>` entry. With a dozen subsystem crates all sitting in the 0.1.x range, patch numbers collide constantly — so `vta-tee` 0.1.0 → 0.1.1 (#819) **passed with no `vta-tee` entry at all**, because `0.1.1` already appeared for `vta-audit`, `vta-backup`, `vta-vault` and `vta-webvh`. It is now on `main` as an undocumented published version; this PR backfills the entry.

A release guard that green-lights an undocumented release is worse than no guard, because it is trusted.

The match now requires the crate name immediately before the version, accepting both heading shapes actually in use:

```
### vta-service 0.12.43 — summary
### vti-secrets 0.1.7 / vta-config 0.1.1 — summary
- `vta-audit` 0.1.1
```

The right-hand token boundary is unchanged, so a `0.1.30` entry still cannot satisfy a bump to `0.1.3`.

**Validation** — replayed the tightened guard over the last 25 commits of `main`, running it at each commit with `BASE=<commit>^`:

- **16** commits carrying version bumps still pass — no false positives.
- **1** new catch: `63539989` (#819), `MISSING vta-tee: 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1`. That is the bug, not a regression.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm` — clean
- `cargo check` in `deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- both release guards pass against `origin/main`

## Versions

`vta-tee` 0.1.1 → **0.1.2**, `vta-service` 0.12.42 → **0.12.45**. The gap is deliberate: #824 claims 0.12.43 and #827 claims 0.12.44, so this stays out of their way regardless of merge order.

title: docs(changelog): say which transports reach the member document form
body:
## What

Corrects one claim in the `vtc-service 0.11.37` entry from #838.

It said *"a client migrating to the document form sees no behaviour change."* That holds over **TSP and REST** and is **false over DIDComm** — which is the reading most likely to be acted on, since DIDComm is what OpenVTC sends these two verbs over today.

## Why it's wrong

`route()` matches on `msg.typ`, so `members/self-remove` and `members/vmc` still reach `member_self_remove_handler` / `member_vmc_handler`, which parse a **bare body**. #838 added the document handlers to `dispatch_trust_task_core`, which DIDComm does not consult for these two types. A sender that switched to the document form without also switching transport would have its document rejected as a malformed bare body.

`join-requests/*` does not have this property — its DIDComm handlers forward to the dispatcher via `inbound_doc_bytes`, so they accept the document on every transport. That asymmetry is exactly what makes the original wording easy to misread.

## The change

- States the reachable transports outright, and names the contrast with `join-requests/*` so the asymmetry is visible.
- Splits the receipt-payload claim — which *does* hold on every transport — into its own bullet, so the two are not read as a single guarantee.

Changelog text only: no code, no version bump. `check-version-bumps.sh` excludes `CHANGELOG*` from the bump requirement; both guards re-run clean.

Refs #838, OpenVTC/openvtc#185

title: feat(vtc): dispatch self-remove and member-VMC as Trust Tasks
body:
## What

#833 gave the VTC a TSP inbound path, but that path reaches a verb **only** through `dispatch_trust_task_core`, whose table was the four `join-requests/*` URIs. The two member-initiated verbs — `members/self-remove` and `members/vmc` — existed only as DIDComm protocol-message handlers taking a bare body.

The practical effect: **a member could join a community over TSP and then not leave over it.** The frame came back `UnsupportedType`.

Both URIs were already canonical Trust Task types under `https://trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/members/`, so this is a routing gap rather than a spec change — the documents were always well-formed, nothing routed them.

## How

- `handle_self_remove` and `handle_member_vmc` run the document form on the **shared spine** — `remove_inner` and `receive_member_vmc_inner`, the same functions the DIDComm handlers call. The two forms therefore cannot drift on policy: the no-last-admin invariant and the VMC issuer/subject + DI-proof checks are enforced where they always were, in the effect stage.
- The proven member comes from `resolve_holder`, so the authenticated identity is the transport's (DIDComm authcrypt sender / TSP sender VID) or the document proof signer — never a self-asserted `issuer`.
- **The bare-body DIDComm handlers stay.** Existing senders keep working, and both forms return the same receipt payload, so a client migrating to the document form sees no behaviour change. Accept before send: the member-side change can only follow this, never precede it.
- `DISPATCHED_URIS` now documents what it had quietly become — the set reachable over TSP, since the TSP path has no protocol-message surface behind it — and its coverage test extends to the member verbs. The module doc no longer claims the dispatcher is join-request-only.
- `parse_disposition` moves from private to `pub(crate)` so both forms reject a bad disposition identically rather than one of them defaulting.

## Why now

Scoping OpenVTC/openvtc#185 (member-side TSP) turned up that only **one** of OpenVTC's four VTC-bound sends could ride TSP today — join submit, which already builds a Trust Task document. Self-remove and member-VMC sent bare bodies with no handler behind them on the Trust Task surface. This is the upstream half; the OpenVTC change follows it.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 693 unit tests + every integration binary, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo check -p vtc-service --locked` — clean (lockfile committed with the bump)
- `scripts/check-version-bumps.sh`, `scripts/check-changelogs.sh` — both pass

Refs OpenVTC/openvtc#185

title: fix(vta-service): resolve self-DID via network-mode resolver in first-enable handshake
body:
## Summary

The transient "first-enable" handshake that trust-pings a newly configured mediator built a **default** TDK config, which resolves DIDs **locally**. In a serverless / network-isolated deployment the agent has no direct network egress, so resolving the mediator DID — and the VTA's own serverless `did:webvh` during mediator authentication — failed with a network error.

## Fix

- Route the first-enable handshake through the VTA's shared **network-mode** resolver (bridged to the parent-side resolver sidecar in an isolated deployment), mirroring the resolver wiring already used by the messaging service and the auth ATM.
- Re-seed the self-DID into the resolver cache immediately before the handshake: webvh cache entries expire after the cache TTL, and a serverless `did:webvh` can only be resolved from cache.

## Changes

- `vta-service/src/routes/protocol.rs` — build the handshake TDK config with the network-mode resolver + re-seed self-DID cache entry (feature-gated on `webvh`).
- `vta-service/src/server.rs` — make `preload_self_did_document` `pub(crate)` so the handshake path can reuse it.

## Testing

`cargo check -p vta-service` (default features: `setup`/`webvh` + `didcomm`) passes.

title: fix: read a join verdict at the nesting the VTC actually sends
body:
## What

A VTC's join verdict never took effect. `handle_join_verdict` deserialized the DIDComm body straight into a `VerdictResponse`, but that is not what arrives — `vtc-service`'s `tt_didcomm_reply` sets the body to the whole `#response` Trust Task **document**, with the task-specific members nested under `payload`:

```json
{ "id": "urn:uuid:…", "threadId": "…", "type": "…#response",
  "payload": { "requestId": "…", "verdict": { "effect": "allow", … } } }
```

`VerdictResponse { request_id, verdict }` has no `payload` member and both fields are required, so the parse failed, the handler logged `malformed join verdict body — ignoring`, and the membership stayed **Pending** — through an `allow` exactly as through a `deny`.

`handle_join_status_response` had the identical defect. Its handler is reached through `dispatch_trust_task_core` + `tt_didcomm_reply` too, so an `approved` status response was dropped the same way.

## Why the tests didn't catch it

They built the **bare payload** as the message body rather than the document the VTC sends — the shape the code expected, not the shape on the wire. Both handlers now have a test that constructs the real `#response` document; each fails without the fix:

```
test verdict_allow_activates ... ok                             ← bare payload (the old fiction)
test verdict_allow_activates_from_response_document ... FAILED  ← the actual wire form
```

## The fix

`trust_task_reply_payload` prefers `payload` when present and takes the body whole otherwise, so both reply shapes reach the same parse.

The two shapes are **not** distinguishable by message type — they are distinguishable by how the VTC built the reply. Anything routed through `dispatch_trust_task_core` comes back as a document; a hand-built `Reply` comes back bare. That is why `join-requests/submit-receipt` is correct as it stands (it is hand-built by `credential_present_handler`) and is deliberately left alone rather than made tolerant for symmetry's sake.

`handle_join_trust_task_error` already read `/payload/code` — it was written against the document form. Two handlers disagreeing about the same wire is what surfaced this.

## Context

Found while scoping #185. TSP delivers that same response document with **no DIDComm envelope around it**, so the handlers had to agree on the document shape before the transport could change under them — the tolerant form is what lets a TSP frame normalise into the existing dispatch unchanged. Fixing it separately because it is a live join-ceremony defect on the DIDComm path today, independent of any TSP work.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` — all binaries green, 0 failed
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc` — clean
- `cargo check --workspace --locked` — clean

Refs #185

title: fix(vta-service): persist auto-generated serverless did:webvh record + log
body:
## Summary

In TEE mode the VTA mints its own `did:webvh` on first boot from the KMS-bootstrapped seed (`tee::did_autogen::maybe_generate_vta_did`) and stores the DID + `did.jsonl` log **only** under the `KEYS`/`BOOTSTRAP` keyspaces. That path never goes through the `create_did_webvh` flow, so the `webvh` keyspace is left empty.

But three read paths resolve the VTA's own DID from the `webvh` keyspace via `webvh_store`:
- `list_services` — reads the record (`did:{did}`) **and** log (`log:{did}`);
- `server::preload_self_did_document` — reads the log to seed the resolver cache;
- `/.well-known/did.jsonl` — reads the log.

So on a serverless TEE VTA, `GET /services` 500s with `VtaDidRecordMissing` and the VTA's own DID is unresolvable from cache — no client can authcrypt to it.

## Fix

Add a small `tee_webvh` bridge in `vta-service` that idempotently backfills the `webvh` keyspace with the record + log after auto-generation, and call it from the enclave startup right after `maybe_generate_vta_did`.

- **Idempotent**: no-op for non-`did:webvh` identities and once the entries exist, so it also repairs an already-generated DID on a rebuild + restore — without wiping state (which would rotate the DID).
- **Record fields** mirror the production serverless builder in `operations::did_webvh::create_did_webvh` (`server_id = "serverless"`, next `#key-{n}` fragment `2`, one pre-rotation key). Any drift self-heals on the next did update/rotate, which re-scans the log and persists corrected counts.
- **Log** is copied from the `KEYS`-keyspace `did.jsonl` the auto-gen already wrote.

Kept in `vta-service` (which owns `webvh_store`) rather than the low-level TEE crate, so that crate doesn't take on a `vta-webvh` dependency.

## Testing

- `cargo check -p vta-service --features tee` passes (compiles the new `#[cfg(feature = "tee")]` module + the enclave feature graph).
- `cargo test -p vta-service --features tee tee_webvh::` — new unit test for the record builder (SCID = 3rd colon-segment, fragment/pre-rotation/log counts) passes.

## Summary

Re-grounds `docs/01-concepts/security-model.md` against the current TEE
implementation. The document had drifted from the code in several places; this
corrects the inaccurate/stale claims and fills gaps, verified against the
implementation.

## Corrections

**Pass 1 — stale/incomplete claims:**
- **KMS attestation (Recipient):** `GenerateDataKey`/`Decrypt` now pass an
  NSM-attested `Recipient`; KMS returns `CiphertextForRecipient` wrapped
  (RSAES-OAEP-SHA256) to an ephemeral in-enclave RSA-2048 key. Updated the
  residual-risk row (was "TODO/not implemented"), the AT1 tree, added a Layer 2

title: perf(deploy/nitro): per-crate COPY layering + full workspace manifest list (#826)
body:
perf(deploy/nitro): per-crate COPY layering + full workspace manifest list (#826)

The Nitro builder stage's dependency-cache warm-up only listed 9 of the
workspace's 26 members, so the manifest-first `cargo build` under-populated
the cache and dependencies were rebuilt from scratch on every image build.
It also copied only a subset of crates for the real build.

Restore selective per-crate manifest + dummy-source + real-source COPYs for
ALL workspace members (kind matched to each manifest: bin/lib/both, plus
vta-mobile-core's uniffi-bindgen bin), and keep deploy/nitro/config.toml baked
only in Stage 2. Editing config now re-layers just the tiny Alpine runtime
stage instead of invalidating the entire Rust dependency cache. Portable — no
BuildKit or cache mounts required.

Notably, the tests-only `tests/e2e` member (`autobins = false`, integration
tests only) has no compile target until its real sources are copied, so it
gets a stub `src/lib.rs` in the warm-up phase purely to satisfy workspace
resolution — without it, `cargo build` fails resolution and the `|| true`
silently swallows the error, giving a full-from-scratch dependency rebuild
every time.

Also exclude enclave signing keys and Nitro runtime state from the build
context (.dockerignore): the build uses selective per-crate COPYs, but adding
`signing/`, `.deploy-nitro/`, and stray `*.txt` avoids shipping private keys
and large EIF artifacts to the Docker daemon.

title: perf(deploy/nitro): per-crate COPY layering + full workspace manifest list
body:
## Summary

The Nitro enclave image (`Dockerfile.nitro`) uses a manifest-first dependency-cache warm-up: copy every crate's `Cargo.toml` + a stub source, run a dummy `cargo build` to compile & cache all external dependencies, then copy the real sources. This only works if the stub phase lists **every** workspace member — otherwise `cargo build` fails workspace resolution, the `|| true` swallows the error, and dependencies are rebuilt from scratch on every image build.

The stub list had drifted to only **9 of the 26** workspace members, and the real-source copy covered the same subset.

## Fix

- List **all** workspace members for both the manifest/stub phase and the real-source copy, with the stub target kind matched to each crate's manifest (bin / lib / both; plus `vta-mobile-core`'s `uniffi-bindgen` bin).
- Keep `deploy/nitro/config.toml` baked only in Stage 2 (runtime). Never `COPY . .` in Stage 1, so editing config re-layers just the tiny Alpine stage instead of invalidating the Rust dependency cache.
- `tests/e2e` (`autobins = false`, integration tests only) has no compile target until its real sources are copied, so it gets a stub `src/lib.rs` in the warm-up phase purely to satisfy workspace resolution. **This was the actual bug** — without a target, `cargo metadata`/`cargo build` fails with `no targets specified in the manifest`.

## `.dockerignore`

Exclude `signing/` (enclave signing cert + private key), `.deploy-nitro/` (EIF artifacts, logs, pidfiles), and stray `*.txt` from the build context — avoids shipping private keys and large EIF artifacts to the Docker daemon.

## Testing

Reconstructed the Stage-1 stub layout (root manifest + `Cargo.lock` + all 26 member manifests + stub sources) in a scratch dir and confirmed `cargo metadata` (full dependency resolution) exits 0 — i.e. the warm-up `cargo build` resolves the workspace instead of silently failing. Verified the member list is an exact 1:1 match with `[workspace].members`.

title: fix(vta-tee): NSM ioctl len field must be u64, not u32 (#819)
body:
fix(vta-tee): NSM ioctl len field must be u64, not u32 (#819)

The Nitro Security Module ioctl expects `struct nsm_iovec { __u64 addr;
__u64 len; }`. Declaring `len` as u32 under #[repr(C)] leaves 4 bytes of
uninitialized padding that the kernel reads as the high bits of the
64-bit length, inflating it to a garbage value and failing the ioctl
with EMSGSIZE (os error 90). Use u64 for both the request and response
buffer lengths.

title: fix(vta-tee): NSM ioctl len field must be u64, not u32
body:
## Summary

Fixes the AWS Nitro Security Module (NSM) ioctl request encoding used by the
enclave attestation path.

## The bug

The NSM ioctl takes `struct nsm_iovec { __u64 addr; __u64 len; }`. The Rust
binding declared `len` as `u32`:

```rust
#[repr(C)]
struct NsmIoBuffer {
    addr: u64,
    len: u32,   // 4 bytes of trailing padding under #[repr(C)]
}
```

Under `#[repr(C)]` the `u32` is followed by 4 bytes of **uninitialized**
padding to satisfy 8-byte alignment. The kernel reads the full 8 bytes as the
`__u64` length, so the padding becomes the high bits — inflating the length to
a garbage value and failing the ioctl with `EMSGSIZE` (os error 90).

## The fix

Declare `len` as `u64` (matching the kernel struct) and widen the two length
assignments accordingly. The struct size is unchanged (`0x20`), so the
`NSM_IOCTL_REQUEST` request code is unaffected.

## Testing

- `cargo check -p vta-tee` passes.
- Verified live on an AWS Nitro Enclave: attestation succeeds and
  `/attestation/status` reports `tee_type: nitro, detected: true`.

---
Opened as a **draft** for review.

title: feat(vtc): accept Trust Tasks over TSP
body:
§6.1/§6.2 of `docs/05-design-notes/tsp-enablement.md` for the VTC — PR 6 of the §13 breakdown. Behind the `tsp` feature, off by default.

## The bug this fixes is a silent drop

TSP frames **already reach the VTC**. The delivery-layer `DidCommTransport` owns the one mediator websocket and surfaces both protocols off it, tagging each `Inbound.message.protocol`. The dispatcher then discarded every TSP frame at its first line:

```rust
let msg: Message = serde_json::from_slice(&inbound.message.payload).ok()?;
```

A TSP payload is Trust-Task bytes, not a DIDComm plaintext — so this returned `None` and the frame vanished **with no log line**.

## What it does

Mirrors `vta-service`'s `messaging::tsp_inbound` + `service::handle_tsp` deliberately rather than inventing a shape: TSP, DIDComm and REST all feed `dispatch_trust_task_core`, so a caller gets identical round-trip semantics whichever transport it arrived on.

- **`Protocol::TSP` → `handle_tsp`**, which dispatches on the shared spine and seals the response back to the proven sender over the same socket (`atm.tsp().send_routed([mediator_did, sender_vid])`). **No second websocket** — the mediator permits one per DID and evicts a second as `duplicate-channel`, which is what flapped the VTA before its standalone loop was removed.
- **Authorization**: the caller is the VID TSP's `unpack` authenticated, and **only** when `verified` is set.
- **Unauthorised → error envelope, not silence.** The VID is cryptographically proven so there's no enumeration exposure, and a conformant client only understands envelopes.
- `JoinTransport::Tsp` records the arrival transport.

## Two decisions worth review

**No plaintext-`from` fallback.** The DIDComm path has one, for two public-read handlers that never authorize on it. TSP has no such reader, so accepting an unproven identity here would only create a way in.

**`tsp_sender` is factored out** so the authorization decision is unit-testable without a mediator socket — the same reason `vta-service` factors out `inbound_gate`. `dispatch_trust_task_core` authorises on its return value, so a wrong answer there is an authorization bug, not a logging one. Three tests pin it: verified sender accepted, unverified refused, anonymous refused.

## Scope: receive-side only

Per §14 Q4 — answering over TSP is required (the caller waits on the TSP correlation), but VTC-**initiated** sends to members stay DIDComm until the Phase B flip (§12).

## Deliberately NOT advertised

The VTC's DID document still carries no `#tsp` service, and must not until this ships. TSP is the **highest-preference** transport, so a VTC advertising it before it could answer would have clients select TSP and get silence — strictly worse than today, and the same false-capability problem the OpenVTC panel work fixed.

Advertising then needs **no code**: it's an `update_did_webvh` service patch on the VTA-managed VTC DID (`operations/did_webvh/update/` already patches arbitrary `/service` blocks). That's the follow-up, and it unblocks OpenVTC/openvtc#185 item 2f.

## Verification

- **Both feature configurations build**: default and `--features tsp`
- **695 lib tests pass in each** (3 new on the authorization gate)
- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` and `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --features tsp -- -D warnings` — both clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo check --workspace --locked` — clean, with `Cargo.lock` committed
- `check-version-bumps.sh` — `ok vtc-service: 0.11.34 -> 0.11.35`; `check-changelogs.sh` — documented

title: feat(credential-exchange): the issuance and presentation family, 0.1
body:
Adds `credential-exchange/{offer,request,issue,query,present}/0.1` and `credential-exchange/pending/{list,approve,deny}/0.1`, plus the shared `credential-exchange/_shared/0.1/deferred-presentation`.

## Why now

These eight URIs are bound and dispatched today by `vta-sdk` / `vta-service` / `vtc-service`, but they resolve to nothing. The five exchange specs exist only as files in the OpenVTC repo while claiming a `trusttasks.org` ID; the three `pending-*` have no spec anywhere. See OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#821 — it is the same published-authority-claim problem that #710 just finished fixing for `spec/vtc/*`, one family later.

## Shape

**The Trust Task is the transport, authentication, threading and relayer envelope; the body is OID4VCI (issuance) or OID4VP + DCQL (presentation).** Those foreign objects are carried verbatim and deliberately **not** re-specified here — re-stating another specification's shape inside this one creates a second source of truth that drifts the moment it revises. `snake_case` members in the schemas (`credential_offer`, `dcql_query`, `vp_token`) are those specifications' own names, not casing drift.

The five exchange tasks are **one-way messages on a thread**, so they declare no `Response` — following `chat/message` and `sync/event`. The `pending/*` trio are request/response and declare one.

## The pending/* trio

When a verifier the holder has not pre-trusted sends a query, the holder neither answers nor refuses — it **defers**, persists the request, and tells the verifier `consentRequired`. These three are how the decision then gets made out of band: list what is waiting, then approve or deny.

They are nested under `pending/` rather than published as flat `pending-list` / `pending-approve` / `pending-deny` siblings of the protocol tasks. The family then reads as what it is: a party-to-party wire protocol, plus an operator surface over the consent backlog it generates.

## Three properties worth reviewing

Each is a rule a plausible implementation gets wrong by default, so each is stated normatively rather than left to inference:

- **`purpose` on a query is REQUIRED and non-empty.** The holder's decision is a consent decision, and consent to an unstated use is not consent. Making it optional would render the well-behaved verifier's query indistinguishable from the one that declines to say — exactly when the difference matters.
- **No wallet enumeration.** Candidates are gathered *only* through the type index named by the query's `meta` discriminator. The consequence is spelled out because it inverts the intuitive reading: a query carrying **no** discriminator contributes **no** candidates. It does not mean "everything". Relatedly, `noMatch` and "held but not consented" must be indistinguishable to the verifier, or refusal itself becomes an enumeration primitive.
- **A denial carries no reason field**, and rejects unknown members. "I don't hold that" and "I hold it and won't show you" have to stay indistinguishable, and a free-text reason is where that leaks.

## pending/approve is `destructive`

Not for what it deletes, but because the disclosure it causes cannot be walked back — there is no revoking a presentation once the verifier holds it.

It mints against the **original** query and nonce. The payload is an `id` and nothing else, so approval is a yes-or-no on a request already made rather than an opportunity to renegotiate it; otherwise the thing approved and the thing presented could differ, which makes the consent record worthless as evidence. An expired deferral MUST be refused rather than re-nonced — silently substituting a fresh nonce presents against a request the verifier has forgotten making, on an authority nobody re-confirmed.

`present/0.1` also states an asymmetry it would be easy to gloss over: plain `eddsa-jcs-2022` has no claim-level selective disclosure, so a holder MUST refuse that path unless the credential's claims are a subset of what was consented to. Over-disclosure there is silent unless explicitly checked for.

## Renumbering and nesting

The five exchange tasks move `1.0` → `0.1`, and `pending-list` → `pending/list`. Both match how the rest of the registry versions and groups its slugs. The consuming repo renames its constants in a follow-up; there are no external consumers, so the wire change is free.

## Also in this PR

Nothing beyond the specs and the regenerated bindings.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 256 specs (248 before), 46 shared schemas
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 302 TS modules
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate` — clean (this is where invalid-example conformance runs; every invalid example is genuinely rejected by its schema)
- `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean
- `tsc --noEmit` — clean

Versions bumped in step: `trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.41, `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.2.41.
