title: feat: route trust tasks over TSP
body:
Closes **#185 item 2b**, unblocked by OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#803 / #810 — **vta-sdk 0.20.2 is published**.

## Why this was blocked, and what changed

TSP was unreachable from OpenVTC for a structural reason, not a missing feature. The only route to a Trust-Task-over-TSP client was `connect_tsp`, which opens its **own** websocket. The mediator permits one per DID and rejects the second with `duplicate-channel` — and the reference VTA points both `#tsp` and `#vta-didcomm` at the same mediator, so the collision was the *normal* case.

0.20.2 makes TSP a **per-surface leg of the existing DIDComm session**. `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` needs no second socket and performs no I/O: TSP send is an HTTP post to the mediator, and TSP receive already arrives on the pickup socket we hold, tagged by protocol. The API also refuses the duplicate-session case outright, so the defect I filed is unrepresentable through it.

## What moves — and what deliberately does not

| Surface | Transport |
|---|---|
| `dispatch_trust_task` — the six `did-management/agent-name` Trust Tasks | **TSP** |
| `get_key_secret`, `create_key`, `create_did_webvh`, `delete_did_webvh`, `list_contexts`, `list_webvh_servers` | **DIDComm, unconditionally** |

Those six have no TSP dispatcher behind them at the VTA. Moving them would break them — which is the whole reason TSP is a per-surface choice rather than a client-wide transport, and why the original framing in #185 (a third `VtaTransport` variant) was wrong.

## Best-effort by construction

Discovery is bounded at 5 s (R1.2), and **every** failure path — no `#tsp` advertised, resolve timeout, resolve error, or a split-mediator topology the API refuses — leaves the client exactly as `connect_auto` returned it: on DIDComm, fully working. TSP is an upgrade; it must never be able to fail a startup that would otherwise have succeeded.

`connect_auto` itself is unchanged in 0.20.2 (verified — no TSP arm), so the bump alters no existing transport selection.

## The panel

`TSP advertised (not yet supported)` → **`TSP for trust tasks`**.

Both the old text and a plain "also available" would now be wrong, in opposite directions: TSP is neither unusable nor an alternative to switch to. It carries part of the traffic while the rest stays on DIDComm, and that third state is what the panel has to express (R6.4). The test asserting the old wording is replaced by one asserting the new state and explicitly rejecting both wrong readings.

## Verification

- All **16** test binaries pass with `--include-ignored`, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` — clean

Also boxed `DegradedOutcome::Joined`: `VtaClient` grew a TSP leg field, so the variant now dwarfs `Exit` — the common outcome — and clippy flagged it.

## Not verified here

No test exercises a trust task actually traversing TSP — that needs a `#tsp`-advertising VTA, and the test mediator fixture does not mint one. The wiring is covered by the panel tests and by the fact that every non-TSP path is unchanged; the leg itself is covered upstream in `tests/e2e/tests/tsp_dual_leg.rs`. Worth a follow-up if the fixture gains a TSP-advertising VTA.

I also could not re-measure the binary-size delta cleanly: the code now calls a `cfg`-gated method, so building without the feature no longer compiles. The earlier figure from #185 (**+148,944 bytes, +0.82%**) was measured on a clean baseline and remains the best estimate for the feature's cost.

title: fix(sdk): TSP is a per-surface leg, not a whole-client transport (#803)
body:
Closes #803. Unblocks OpenVTC/openvtc#185 item 2b.

## The problem

A consumer holding a DIDComm session could not use TSP at all. The only route to a
Trust-Task-over-TSP client was `connect_tsp`, which opens its **own** websocket — and
the mediator permits one websocket per DID, so the second was rejected with
`duplicate-channel` and the two reconnect loops duelled. On the reference deployment
`#tsp` and `#vta-didcomm` resolve to the *same* mediator, so this was the normal case.

## What decided the design

**The VTA already fixed this on the server side.** `vta-service/src/server.rs:1056-1062`
deleted its standalone TSP websocket because it "made the mediator evict a connection as
`duplicate-channel`, flapping the VTA"; it now demuxes TSP off its single delivery-layer
socket. This PR is the client-side mirror of a fix already in production.

**The plumbing was already there and unused.** `DidCommTransport::inbound` polls
`live_stream_next_frame`, which yields **both** protocols off the one pickup socket and
tags each `Inbound` with `message.protocol`. TSP *send* is an HTTP `POST /inbound` — no
socket at all. So a full TSP leg on an existing DIDComm session costs **zero new sockets**.

## Changes

- **`DIDCommSession` TSP leg** — `send_tsp_document` / `request_tsp` / `receive_next_tsp`
  over the existing connection. The leg takes its own `subscribe()` receiver (subscribers
  are a broadcast), so the TSP pump cannot eat a DIDComm push and `receive_next` cannot eat
  a TSP reply.
- **`VtaClient::enable_tsp_trust_tasks`** — the seam #803 asks for. Moves the Trust-Task
  surface (`dispatch_trust_task`, `rpc_tt`, the `device/*` and `vault/*` methods) onto TSP.
  No I/O, cannot fail. `attach_tsp_leg` covers the split-mediator topology and **refuses**
  a second session for a DID on the mediator it is already connected to — the defect is
  unrepresentable through the API. `connect_didcomm_with_tsp` does both in one call.
- `rpc` / `rpc_void` stay on DIDComm unconditionally — the VTA has no TSP dispatcher behind
  `key-management/1.0/*`, `create_did_webvh` or `list_contexts`.
- **`SurfaceTransport` + `trust_task_transport()` / `protocol_message_transport()`** — a
  client no longer has *one* transport, so an operator display rendering a single value is
  wrong by construction (openvtc#185 item 2a).

### Live regression fixed on the pnm/cnm path

`TransportChoice::Auto` returned a **TSP-only** client whenever a VTA advertised `#tsp`,
so on a TSP-enabled VTA every protocol-message command (`keys create`, `contexts list`,
DID minting) failed with `UnsupportedTransport`. Auto now returns a **dual** client against
a VTA advertising both — one socket — and still falls back to TSP-only, loudly, when the
DIDComm mediator is down. Forced `--transport tsp` is unchanged (TSP-only by request).

### Also fixed

`DIDCommSession::receive_next` parsed every inbound frame as a DIDComm `Message`, so a TSP
frame on the multiplexed socket became a hard error on the DIDComm inbox that received it.
Latent on `main` only because nothing sent TSP to an SDK DIDComm session.

Reply correlation moved to a shared `tsp_demux` so `TspSession` and the new leg cannot
drift on the rule that stops a *stale* inbox frame being returned as a reply (#749). Its
parking queue is now bounded (previously unbounded).

## Verification

**Live, against the deployed VTA** (`glenn-vta`, both services on one mediator) — a trust
task dispatched over the DIDComm session's socket reached the VTA and its reply came back
correlated:

```
  TSP mediator:     did:webvh:QmTS3a…:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
  DIDComm mediator: did:webvh:QmTS3a…:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
  ✅ TSP on the DIDComm session's socket: the VTA answered
  ✅ DIDComm (control): the VTA answered
```

`vta-sdk/tests/tsp_dual_leg_live.rs` (`#[ignore]`d, credential-free — a `permissionDenied`
trust-task *response* proves the transport; only a transport error fails it. Set
`VTA_LIVE_CLIENT_DID`/`_KEY` to tighten to a successful payload).

**Hermetic, in CI** — `tests/e2e/tests/tsp_dual_leg.rs` over the embedded `TestMediator`
(4 tests, all green): a TSP frame reaches a DID whose only connection is a `DIDCommSession`;
both legs work on that one session; `request_tsp` correlates its reply while an unrelated
push is parked, not eaten; and the API refuses the duplicate socket.

Plus unit coverage for the demux (correlation, nonce fallback, parking, concurrency,
bounded queue) and leg selection, `Send`-future assertions for the new call chain, `cargo
fmt`, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean.

`vta-sdk` 0.20.1 → 0.20.2 — additive only; a minor bump would break the workspace
`[patch.crates-io]` pin.

title: TSP: a consumer already holding a DIDComm session cannot use TSP — connect_tsp opens a second socket and the mediator rejects it (duplicate-channel)
body:
`vta-sdk` can construct a Trust-Task-over-TSP `VtaClient` only by opening its
**own** websocket. Any consumer that already holds a DIDComm session on the same
client DID therefore cannot use TSP at all: the mediator rejects the second
socket with `duplicate-channel`.

This blocks OpenVTC/openvtc#185 item 2b (route OpenVTC's trust-task surface over
TSP). Everything below is from trying to implement it.

**Verified against `origin/main` at cbfc3f83**, not just the published crate — the
in-tree `vta-sdk` is also `0.20.0`, `connect_tsp` still calls
`TspSession::connect`, `connect_auto` has no TSP arm, and there is no constructor
taking an existing session. So #797 (which closed #765/#766/#767) does not cover
this; it made TSP selectable for the session-store path, and this is the gap that
remains for every other consumer.

## The collision

`TspSession::connect` (`vta-sdk/src/session.rs:2233`) builds its own
`TDKSharedState`, its own `ATM`, its own `ATMProfile` for `client_did`, and calls
`atm.tsp().connect_websocket(&profile)`:

```rust
let atm = ATM::new(ATMConfig::builder().build()?, Arc::new(tdk)).await?;
let profile = ATMProfile::new(&atm, None, client_did.to_string(),
                              Some(mediator_did.to_string())).await?;
let ws = atm.tsp().connect_websocket(&profile).await?;
```

`VtaClient::connect_tsp` wraps that in `Transport::Tsp`, so there is no way to
obtain a TSP-capable `VtaClient` other than opening a fresh socket.

**The mediator permits one websocket per DID**, rejecting a second with
`duplicate-channel` — documented in `design-docs/vti-phase3-cutover-plan.md` §4
(investigated 2026-07-16), and restated in
`affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service/src/config.rs:14`:

> The mediator allows one websocket per DID, so a node speaking both protocols
> multiplexes them on the same socket rather than opening a second one.

A consumer holding a DIDComm session on `client_did` (the normal shape — the SDK's
own `LeakGuard` discipline is one `DIDCommSession` per `client_did`) cannot open a
`TspSession` on that same DID against that same mediator.

## It is the normal case, not an edge case

`Transport::Tsp`'s doc notes the TSP mediator is *"not assumed to equal the
DIDComm mediator"*, so a split-mediator deployment would dodge this. The
reference deployment does not split. Resolving
`did:webvh:QmWoJD2kpP6AJknNtj7UFERUstEen258ywj3ruHoh1ZAqr:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta`:

```
#tsp           TSPTransport      -> did:webvh:QmTS3a3H9Dk4ZMPAZ8jNWGeyPbuKrPbrPZcSbg8CJ6yynD:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
#vta-didcomm   DIDCommMessaging  -> did:webvh:QmTS3a3H9Dk4ZMPAZ8jNWGeyPbuKrPbrPZcSbg8CJ6yynD:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
```

Same mediator. So enabling TSP on a consumer that already speaks DIDComm produces
two sockets on one DID against one mediator.

Worth stating plainly: because the split-mediator topology *would* work, this is
the worst failure shape available — correct on an unusual deployment,
`duplicate-channel` plus duelling auto-reconnect loops on the reference one. That
is a diagnosis cost paid by whoever enables TSP next, and the symptom (a dropped
response on the first burst of requests) points nowhere near the cause.

## Why a consumer cannot work around it

- **Drop the DIDComm session while using TSP.** Not viable: TSP carries the
  Trust-Task surface only. `rpc`/`rpc_void` operations — `key-management/1.0/*`,
  `create_did_webvh`, `list_contexts`, `list_webvh_servers` — return
  `UnsupportedTransport` over TSP by design (`client/mod.rs:161`). A consumer needs
  both legs live simultaneously, which is exactly what the one-socket rule forbids
  across two sessions.
- **Use a different DID for the TSP session.** Changes the proven `sender_vid` the
  VTA authorizes against, so it is a different principal — not a workaround, a
  different security posture.
- **Reach TSP through the messaging layer instead.**
  `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` 0.3.20 already does the right thing:
  `Protocols::BOTH` multiplexes DIDComm + TSP on **one** socket, with a
  `TspHandler` symmetric to `DIDCommHandler`. But that socket is owned by
  `AffinidiMessageService`, and `VtaClient` has no constructor that accepts one —
  so a consumer can receive TSP frames there while still being unable to
  `dispatch_trust_task` over TSP.

That last point is the gap: the multiplexing already exists one layer down. What
is missing is the seam between it and `VtaClient`.

## Proposed direction

Either would unblock the consumer; (1) looks cheaper and composes with what
already exists.

1. **A `VtaClient` constructor over an existing multiplexed session** — e.g.
   `VtaClient::over_tsp_session(Arc<TspSession>, vta_did, mediator_did, rest_url)`,
   or accepting the messaging layer's socket, so the single multiplexed socket
   carries `dispatch_trust_task`. The consumer keeps one socket per DID and
   chooses per surface.

2. **`connect_auto` multiplexing both protocols itself** — one client, `rpc` on the
   DIDComm leg and `rpc_tt`/`dispatch_trust_task` on the TSP leg, with
   `Transport::Tsp`'s current all-or-nothing behaviour becoming the
   TSP-only-deployment case. This removes the per-surface decision from every
   consumer, at the cost of a larger change to `Transport`.

Whichever lands, the `TransportChoice` policy already written for
`SessionStore::connect_with_transport` (TSP > DIDComm > REST, bounded connects via
`TSP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT`, deliberately loud fallback) should apply to it
rather than being re-derived — consumers not on the session-store path currently
cannot reach any of it.

## Notes

- Related: #765 / #766 / #767 (all closed) delivered discovery, `TransportChoice`,
  and the correlated request/response client. This is the remaining piece for a
  consumer that is not the `pnm`/`cnm` session-store path.
- Consumer-side context and the full investigation: OpenVTC/openvtc#185.
- Enabling the `tsp` feature itself is cheap: **+148,944 bytes, +0.82%** on the
  OpenVTC release binary (18,112,368 → 18,261,312; macOS arm64, `lto = true`,
  `strip = "symbols"`), building clean. Binary size is not what is holding this up.

title: refactor(vtc): admin passkeys move to the canonical auth/passkey tasks
body:
The VTI half of [trust-tasks-tf#145](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/145). Moves `/v1/admin/passkeys/*` off the retired `openvtc/vtc/` authority onto the canonical tasks that PR published (`trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.38 → 0.2.39).

**Three of the eight entries in `AWAITING_CANONICAL_FOLD` are gone.** #710 and #709 shrink accordingly; five remain.

## No wire change

The canonical specs were written **from this implementation**, not the other way round. Request and response bodies are byte-identical — only the `type` URIs moved.

## One task per ceremony leg, where there used to be one per family

`admin/passkeys/register/1.0` covered *both* `register/start` and `register/finish`; `revoke/1.0` likewise. A single schema spanning both legs has to permit the union of their members — which means **a `finish` arriving without its user-verification assertion still validated against the family task**. Each leg now names its own:

| Endpoint | Task |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/admin/passkeys` | `auth/passkey/list/0.1` |
| `POST …/register/start` | `auth/passkey/enroll/start/0.2` |
| `POST …/register/finish` | `auth/passkey/enroll/finish/0.2` |
| `POST …/revoke/start` | `auth/passkey/revoke/start/0.1` |
| `POST …/revoke/finish` | `auth/passkey/revoke/finish/0.1` |

## Every call site audited per leg, not renamed in bulk

A mount split means a bulk find-and-replace is exactly the wrong move — that's how splitting the VTC mounts earlier hid two admin-UI bugs. So all four binding sites were walked individually, each call site mapped to the endpoint it actually targets before being repointed:

- the router (5 mounts)
- `tests/admin_passkeys.rs` — **19 call sites**
- `tests/install_flow.rs` — 3
- `admin-ui/src/plugins/myPasskeys.tsx` — 4

The negative test that deliberately sends the wrong task to `register/start` still sends a wrong one.

## The recorded blocker was wrong

This is why these three sat unfolded so long. The note said each needed a **`confirm/1.0` gate**. Reading that spec: `confirm/request` is an **asynchronous** delegation whose response returns *out of band on the approver's own transport*. That is right when the approver is a separate party. It is wrong here — this surface verifies the user **in-band, in the same request**, via WebAuthn, and always did.

`enroll/*` moves to **0.2** because that is the version carrying the optional `uvOptions` / `uvCredential` members describing the re-authentication half this code already performs.

Worth noting for whoever picks up the rest: **`members/promote-to-admin` carries the same wrong blocker.** It is also a synchronous two-phase UV ceremony (`promote_start` / `promote_finish`). It is *not* a free fold though — its `finish` leg is fused, consuming the UV assertion *and* performing the role change, and `acl/change-role/0.1` requires `{subject, fromRole, toRole}` which the endpoint never carries. It needs either an API split or a new spec; both are judgement calls, not mechanical work.

## Retiring the superseded tasks

The manifest test refuses to publish a task no route binds, so `admin/passkeys/{list,register,revoke}/1.0` are marked `status: retired` + `supersededBy` in `trust-tasks/` and `index.json`, per SPEC §5.3 — the same treatment `admin/config/manage` got.

- `cargo check --workspace --locked --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — full suite green
- `trust_task_manifest` 7/7 · `admin_passkeys` 12/12 · `install_flow` 1/1
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — no warnings
- `cargo fmt --check`, version-bump guard, changelog guard, lockfile self-pin guard — all pass

title: feat: rebuild a listener whose ATM has died
body:
Closes the gap I named in #194 rather than filled at the time.

## What was missing

`DidCommTransport::inbound()` survives a socket drop — the ATM reconnects underneath it — so ordinary churn needs no supervision. What it cannot survive is **the ATM task itself dying**: the transport is then permanently `Disconnected` with nothing retrying behind it, and the listener is stranded until the process restarts. The framework's `RestartPolicy` used to cover that; the delivery layer has no equivalent.

## The hard part is not rebuilding — it's not rebuilding too eagerly

`ConnState::Disconnected` means *"dropped, retrying or idle"*, not *"gone"*. A supervisor that reacted to it would open a second websocket for a DID whose ATM is already retrying, and the mediator rejects the second with `duplicate-channel` — **manufacturing the duelling-reconnect fault the supervisor exists to recover from** (#132).

So the grace period being generous *is* the safety property, not conservatism:

- **`REBUILD_GRACE` (90 s)** must exceed the window a healthy reconnect needs. A test asserts it also exceeds the backoff ceiling, so a rebuild can never be scheduled sooner than a normal recovery would have finished.
- **Backoff 5 s → 10 s → 20 s → 40 s, capped at 60 s** — the framework's old policy, including `max_retries: None`. A mediator that returns hours later is picked up without restarting the app.
- **Remove before add**, for the same one-socket-per-DID reason.
- A listener removed *deliberately* (community left, DID deleted) between the state sample and the rebuild is dropped from tracking, not resurrected.

`IdentityWire` now retains its `ListenerSpec`, since rebuilding means constructing a fresh ATM, profile and transport from the same inputs.

## Why the policy is two pure functions

`rebuild_due` and `rebuild_backoff` are split out of the loop because that is where the entire risk lives — too eager causes `duplicate-channel`, never causes a stranded listener — and a pure function is something tests can pin in **both** directions. Six unit tests do, including that a drop one second old is left alone, and that a day-long outage still retries.

The integration test earns its keep separately: over a real mediator, across several supervisor ticks, a connected listener reports no disconnect transition and stays `Connected`. **A supervisor that rebuilt on every tick would pass every unit test and fail this one.**

## Verification

- All **16** test binaries pass with `--include-ignored`, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` — clean

## Still not covered, and I'd rather say so

No test kills an ATM and observes a real rebuild — I could not find a way to tear one down from outside the SDK without reaching into its internals. So the *trigger* is verified by construction and by the policy tests; the *rebuild path itself* shares its code with `add_listener`, which the other e2e tests exercise. If you know a way to kill an ATM cleanly in the test mediator, that would close the last of it.

title: fix(specs): relative links resolve, and a guard so they keep resolving
body:
136 broken relative links across 65 `spec.md` files — plus the check that should have caught them.

## What was wrong

Relative links in spec prose resolve from the **version** directory (`specs/<slug>/<version>/`), because that is where `spec.md` lives and where it is served from — `build-registry.mjs` syncs `specs/` verbatim to `website/specs/<slug>/<version>/`.

135 of the 136 were written as though they resolved from the **slug** directory, one level shallower. From `auth/passkey/enroll/start/0.1`, `../finish/0.1/spec.md` points at `.../start/finish/0.1/`, which has never existed.

**These were broken on the live site, not merely in the repo.**

The single outlier was not a depth error at all: `vtc/policies/test` linked to `vtc/policies/upload`, which does not exist under *any* depth. That task was repointed onto the canonical `policy/upsert/0.2` (VTI #729) and the link never followed. Retargeted rather than mechanically deepened.

`bindings/` was already clean and is unchanged.

## The guard is the point

A sweep without one regresses immediately — 135 links drifted the same way precisely because nothing checked. `build-registry.mjs` now resolves every relative markdown link and fails the build on a miss. When the target resolves one level deeper, it says so, because that is the mistake people will actually make:

```
auth/passkey/list/0.1/spec.md: relative link '../revoke/start/0.1/spec.md' does not
resolve — one level too shallow; '../../revoke/start/0.1/spec.md' resolves
```

Verified **both** directions: a clean build across all 246 specs, and a deliberately reintroduced break failing with exactly the message above.

## No version bump

Codegen drift is **zero** — the bindings generate from `payload.schema.json`, and this touches only prose and the build script. Confirmed with `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`: no diff under `trust-tasks-rs/src` or `trust-tasks-ts/src`.

title: feat: run OpenVTC messaging on the delivery layer
body:
Closes #189. **OpenVTC no longer depends on `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` at all** — the type-routed framework both VTI services had already cut away from.

## The shape change

The old framework owned N *listeners* and hid packing, retry and routing behind them. The delivery layer owns N *transports keyed by identity*, and the transport determines the proven sender — so "send as this persona" is `send_via(persona_did, …)` rather than a listener lookup, and packing is the caller's job because `MessageTransport::send` takes already-packed bytes.

- **`Messaging` replaces `DIDCommService`** — one `MessagingService`, one `DidCommTransport` per identity, a shared `via`-partitioned outbox, per-identity drains. Cloneable, since call sites hand it to spawned tasks.
- **`add_listener`** brings up one identity's wire in the order the SDK requires: secrets seeded *before* `ATM::new`, profile via `from_tdk_profile`, `profile_add(_, true)` to connect the websocket, then `DidCommTransport::new` — which fails on a profile with no websocket running.
- **`dispatch_inbound` replaces `Router`** — the delivery layer has no type-routed dispatch, so the catch-all regex, trust-ping/pong and the drop cases are matched here. It prefers the transport's **cryptographically-bound** sender over the plaintext `from` header, which the framework did not.
- **One connection poller broadcasts `ListenerStatus`**, consumed by both the session manager and the activity log, so the two cannot disagree about whether a listener is up. Read live, never latched at boot (R6.2).
- **`start_service` installs listeners one at a time** — each is an independent mediator connect, so one persona whose mediator is down no longer stops the others coming up.

## Two decisions worth review

**`Delivery::Guaranteed`, not `BestEffort`.** `send_message_with_retry` retried on a disconnected listener; `BestEffort` has no retry. A straight swap would have traded a retry for a message dropped whenever a send landed mid-reconnect — in a TUI, exactly when someone presses a key. The outbox is that retry and survives the reconnect; the delivery window bounds it (R1.2) so an entry settles visibly rather than never.

**`reconnect_persona_listener_io` removes before it adds.** The mediator permits one websocket per DID and rejects a second with `duplicate-channel`, so add-before-remove would race two sockets on one identity — the duelling-reconnect failure behind #132. The reason is in the code, not just here.

`MessagingError` replaces `DIDCommServiceError` with variants an operator can act on separately — listener-bringup, unknown-listener, pack, send (R6.4). `remove_listener` is now infallible (dropping a transport cannot fail), so four call sites lose dead error handling.

## Verification

- **All 16 test binaries pass** with `--include-ignored`, 0 failed
- `didcomm_transport_e2e` drives the production `Messaging`, `add_listener`, dispatcher and `Guaranteed` send **against a real mediator**, asserting an OpenVTC type routes through to the event channel and an unrelated one reaches no handler
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` — clean

## What this does not cover, honestly

The e2e test exercises listener bringup, routing and send. It does **not** exercise a mediator dropping a live socket and the transport recovering — `DidCommTransport::inbound()` stays alive across reconnects (verified by reading the adapter), but a full ATM task teardown would leave the transport stale where the framework's `RestartPolicy` rebuilt it. **No such rebuild is implemented here.** `transport_state` is the signal it would key off, and I'd rather land the swap with that gap named than paper it with logic no test covers. Worth a follow-up issue if you agree.

## Follow-on

TSP **inbound** is now one feature flag away: `DidCommTransport` surfaces TSP frames off this same multiplexed pickup socket tagged `Protocol::TSP`, with no second socket — which is what sidesteps the `duplicate-channel` wall blocking #185 item 2b. The dispatcher currently skips non-DIDComm payloads; routing them is #185's remaining work.

title: Decide which messaging layer OpenVTC targets: affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service has been replaced upstream
body:
OpenVTC builds its DIDComm listeners on `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service`.
Both VTI services have cut over to `affinidi-messaging-delivery`, and one of them
describes the framework we use as *removed*. We should decide deliberately which
layer OpenVTC targets, rather than discovering it when the old crate stops moving.

Surfaced while investigating #185 item 2f, which wanted to add TSP wiring to the
old framework. That is what made this worth its own issue: the choice of layer
decides whether that work is written once or twice.

## What changed upstream

Verified against VTI `origin/main` @ cbfc3f83.

- **`vtc-service`** — *"D1 delivery layer (P1a cut-over): `MessagingService`
  (subscribe/send) over a `DidCommTransport`, **replacing the old
  `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service`** type-routed framework"*
  (`vtc-service/Cargo.toml:122-124`). And `messaging.rs:47-50`: *"These used to
  come from the `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` framework; **with that
  framework removed** (the delivery-layer cut-over, D2 P1a) we re-declare the two
  we act on."*
- **`vta-service`** — *"D2 P2a cut-over: the reliable-messaging delivery layer
  replaces the old `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` type-routed framework"*
  (`vta-service/Cargo.toml:182-183`).

In both crates the remaining mentions are **comments explaining the
replacement**, not dependencies.

The old crate is not yanked — `0.3.20` is still the latest published, and it is
what we pin (`Cargo.toml:29`). So nothing is broken today. The exposure is that
OpenVTC is now the party still building on it.

## What OpenVTC uses from it

Small surface, which is the good news:

| Item | Uses |
|---|---|
| `DIDCommService` | 8 |
| `HandlerContext` | 5 |
| `handler_fn` | 4 |
| `ListenerEvent` | 2 |
| `Router`, `ListenerConfig`, `ListenerState`, `RestartPolicy`, `RetryConfig`, `DIDCommServiceConfig`, `DIDCommServiceError`, `TRUST_PING_TYPE`, `TRUST_PONG_TYPE` | 1 each |

Concentrated almost entirely in `openvtc/src/state_handler/didcomm.rs`.

## What the delivery layer would give us

`affinidi-messaging-delivery` 0.1.11 is a different shape: not a type-routed
handler framework but a reliable-delivery front-end.

- **A durable outbox with real delivery states.** `Delivery::{BestEffort,
  Guaranteed{idempotency_key, ordering_key, deliver_by}}`, entries moving
  `Queued → Sent → Delivered | Unconfirmed | Failed`, drain with backoff.
- **`Sent::{Accepted, Delivered, Unconfirmed}`** — the crate's own words: *"so a
  caller can no longer log a merely-queued message as delivered"*. **We have
  already hand-rolled this distinction.** #141 added an awaiting-receipt indicator
  for unacknowledged `Pending` joins precisely because a submitted join that was
  never acknowledged looked identical to one in flight. `Unconfirmed` is that
  state, in the layer.
- **Idempotency keys**, which is what a re-submitted join needs to not double-join.
- **`MessagingStatus::{Connected, Degraded, Disconnected}`** read off live
  `connection_state()`, *"never a boot-time latch"*.

Relevant history: the dropped join submit in #137 (a bridge size limit silently
losing the message), the stuck-`Pending` joins behind #139/#141, and the
duelling-session timeout in #132 are all delivery-reliability faults that this
layer exists to make visible rather than silent.

## What we would have to rebuild

- **Type-routed dispatch.** There is no `Router`/`handler_fn` equivalent;
  `vtc-service` re-declared its own type constants and dispatches itself. Our
  `OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` regex routing would move into our own dispatcher.
- **Listener lifecycle.** `ListenerEvent` (Connected/Disconnected, and the
  rapid-cycling detection in `spawn_lifecycle_logger`) maps onto `ConnState` /
  `MessagingStatus`, but not one-to-one — the rapid-cycling heuristic is ours.
- **`RestartPolicy` / `RetryConfig`.** Partly subsumed by drain/backoff, partly not.

## The crux: OpenVTC is multi-identity, and the new layer's N is not that N

This is the real design question and the reason this is an issue rather than a PR.

`build_listener_configs` (`didcomm.rs:339`) creates **one listener per persona
identity** — each with its own DID, its own mediator, its own secrets and profile
— plus `rel-*` listeners for relationship DIDs. One websocket per DID, which is
also the mediator's hard rule (`duplicate-channel`).

`MessagingService` is *"N transports + one outbox with a single merged inbound
dispatcher"* — but that N is for **mediator lifecycle** (migrate / rollback /
drain) over one identity, with outbound through the current primary. It is not N
identities. `vtc-service` instantiates exactly one, on the VTC DID
(`messaging.rs:210`), so it is **not** a template for our case.

So, undecided and needing a decision before any code:

1. **One `MessagingService` per DID** (N services, N outboxes) — closest to today's
   model, but multiplies the outbox/drain machinery and leaves "who merges the
   inbound streams" to us.
2. **One service, multi-identity** — needs a concept the layer does not currently
   have, i.e. upstream work.
3. **Stay on the old framework** for now and revisit — legitimate if the old crate
   keeps receiving the fixes we need, and it is the only option that costs nothing
   today.

## Why this gates the TSP story

`affinidi-messaging-core`'s transport contract is explicitly *"DIDComm today, TSP
and REST later"*, and `TransportKind` already reserves `Tsp`
(`affinidi-messaging-core/src/transport.rs:45-49`). So TSP is planned **on the
delivery layer**.

Meanwhile the old framework's `Protocols::BOTH` + `TspHandler` — the thing #185
item 2f was going to use — multiplexes TSP on one socket *today*, but on the
framework both services have left.

Which means: **item 2f should not be built until this is decided.** On the old
framework it is work that gets thrown away; on the new one it does not exist yet.
This is recorded on #185, which is otherwise fully blocked (item 2b needs
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#803, and the VTC does not advertise `#tsp`
at all yet).

## Asks

- [ ] Decide between (1), (2) and (3) above — the multi-identity question is the
      blocker, not the API surface.
- [ ] If not (3): confirm with the VTI side whether a multi-identity
      `MessagingService` is intended, or whether one-service-per-DID is the
      expected consumer shape. Worth asking before we pick, since we would be the
      first multi-identity consumer.
- [ ] Confirm whether `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` is still maintained for
      consumers, or effectively frozen at 0.3.20. That single answer decides how
      urgent (3) is.
- [ ] Sequence against #185 either way, so TSP lands on the chosen layer once.

No code changes proposed here — this is a direction decision, and the
multi-identity mapping is not something to guess at.

    the delivery window bounds it (R1.2) so an entry settles visibly
    rather than never.

  * One connection poller broadcasts ListenerStatus, consumed by both the
    session manager and the activity log, so the two cannot disagree
    about whether a listener is up. States are read live, never latched
    at boot (R6.2).

  * start_service installs listeners one at a time: each is an
    independent mediator connect, so one persona whose mediator is down
    no longer stops the others coming up.

reconnect_persona_listener_io removes before it adds, with the reason
written down: the mediator permits one websocket per DID and rejects a
second with duplicate-channel, so add-before-remove would race two
sockets on one identity -- the duelling-reconnect failure behind #132.

MessagingError replaces DIDCommServiceError with variants an operator can
act on separately: listener-bringup, unknown-listener, pack, send (R6.4).
remove_listener is now infallible -- dropping a transport cannot fail --
so four call sites lose dead error handling.

didcomm_transport_e2e, which drives the production Messaging, add_listener,
dispatcher and Guaranteed send against a real mediator and asserts an
OpenVTC type routes through while an unrelated one reaches no handler.

Closes #189

title: feat(auth): passkey list + revoke, and re-authenticated enrollment
body:
Three new tasks plus one version bump. These are the upstream half of closing [OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#710](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/issues/710) — the VTC's `admin/passkeys/*` surface is stranded on the retired `openvtc/vtc/` authority because the canonical specs did not exist. Now they do; the VTI-side repoint follows separately.

## `auth/passkey/list/0.1`

The credential-management counterpart to `auth/sessions/list`. Sessions answers *"where am I signed in?"*; this answers *"what can sign me in?"* — longer-lived and more consequential, because revoking a session ends an episode while revoking a credential removes a capability.

**No subject filter.** The subject comes from the `proof`. That removes the class of bug where a filter parameter and an authorization check disagree.

**Deliberately omits** public key, signature counter and AAGUID. None help a human pick which authenticator to revoke; the counter is cloning-detection telemetry that belongs in the consumer's own logs.

## `auth/passkey/revoke/{start,finish}/0.1`

Removal behind a fresh WebAuthn user-verification ceremony — two legs, mirroring `enroll/*`.

**On not using `confirm/1.0`.** The VTI design note this came from assumed a delegated `confirm` gate. Reading that spec: `confirm/request` is *asynchronous*, and its response arrives out of band on the approver's own transport. That is the right shape when the approver is a separate party. It is the wrong shape here — the approver *is* the subject, already mid-ceremony, and it would make revocation depend on a second transport being reachable at the exact moment somebody is trying to eject a stolen authenticator. So the confirmation stays in-band and synchronous, reusing the WebAuthn stack that already authenticates. Consumers whose approver genuinely is a separate party are pointed at `confirm/*` via `ext`.

**Two properties worth your attention:**

1. **The target is bound to the `revocationId` server-side**, so `finish` carries no credential of its own — and the invalid-examples pin that. Accepting a copy at finish would let an intercepted ceremony be redirected: the user verifies one credential and a different one is destroyed.

2. **The last-credential refusal is normative and checked at *both* legs.** Start's check fails fast so the subject is not walked through a doomed ceremony; finish's check is the one that actually holds the invariant, since a concurrent revocation can complete in the gap. Checking only at start is a race with a window as long as the ceremony timeout. Both, with only the second load-bearing, is the shape that is correct and humane at once.

`user_verification_failed` covers bad signature, wrong challenge, wrong origin and clear UV flag alike — separating them hands an attacker the map of which control stopped them.

## `auth/passkey/enroll/{start,finish}` → 0.2

Adds optional `uvOptions` (start response) and `uvCredential` (finish request), so a consumer can require an **existing** authenticator to authorize adding a new one.

0.1 modelled enrollment as a single ceremony authorized by the `proof`. That is right for a *first* passkey and wrong for a subsequent one: silently enrolling an attacker-controlled authenticator is durable access that survives the subject changing everything else, and it looks like a legitimate device in `list`. Optional, because a first enrollment has nothing to verify against.

**0.1 stays published and unchanged.** A 0.1 producer against a 0.2 consumer that issues `uvOptions` fails at finish — intended, versus a consumer silently dropping a control it decided it needed.

## Shared schema

`RegisteredCredential` added to `auth/_shared/0.1/webauthn.schema.json`. **Additive — no existing `$def` changed** (35 insertions, 0 deletions).

**`lastUsedAt` is a plain optional, not a nullable.** The first draft distinguished "tracked and never used" from "not tracked", and the generated-binding round-trip test rejected it: absent and null map onto the same `Option`. A distinction the reference implementation cannot represent is not one a conforming consumer could rely on, so it is gone rather than papered over. Worth flagging as a general constraint on schema design here.

## A pre-existing defect found on the way, NOT fixed here

Relative links in the new specs resolve correctly from the version directory. The 0.1 enroll/login specs these were modelled on are **off by one level** in their `SPEC.md`, `_shared/` and sibling-leg links — `../finish/0.1/spec.md` from `enroll/start/0.1/` resolves to `enroll/start/finish/0.1/`, which does not exist. The 0.2 copies correct it.

The same class of broken link exists in **~69 spec directories repo-wide**, including several I authored in #144. Since `build-registry.mjs` syncs `specs/` verbatim to `website/specs/<slug>/<version>/`, they are broken on the live site too. Left for a separate sweep rather than buried in this PR — happy to take it next.

## Verification

- `npm run build` — 246 specs validated, 44 shared schemas indexed
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — no drift beyond the three `mod.rs` files gaining submodules
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 290 TS modules
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features` — **502 passed, 0 failed**
- Both libraries bumped 0.2.38 → 0.2.39, `Cargo.lock` refreshed, changelog names the version

title: refactor: describe listeners with ListenerSpec, not the framework type
body:
Preparation for the delivery-layer swap (#189). **No behaviour change.**

## Why

Four call sites built listener configs as struct literals of `ListenerConfig` — an `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` type — and three more passed it across module and crate boundaries.

The swap replaces that type with an ATM profile plus a `DidCommTransport`, and the two have no common constructor. So every one of those sites would have had to change *in the same commit that rewires the transport* — a diff where the interesting change (sockets, reconnect, dispatch) is buried among mechanical edits. That is exactly the shape a messaging regression hides in, and this module's failure mode is `duplicate-channel` plus duelling reconnect loops, which no test would flag.

## What

The framework type is now confined to one function body.

- **`ListenerSpec`** describes a listener by what it *is* — id, DID, mediator, label, secrets — with no reference to what runs it. `Debug` is hand-written so the secrets are never rendered.
- **`ListenerSpec::to_listener_config`** is the single place `ListenerConfig` is constructed, and it is private.
- **`didcomm::add_listener(service, spec)`** is the public way to install one, so callers outside the module never name the framework type. At the swap its body becomes "build a profile + `DidCommTransport` and `add_transport`", and **no caller changes**.

The four builders — `build_listener_configs`' two arms, `persona_listener_config`, `persona_listener_config_for`, `relationship_listener_config_from_secrets` — now return `ListenerSpec`, and `reconnect_persona_listener_io` takes one.

`ListenerConfig` appears in **one** function body where it previously appeared in seven places across three crates' worth of call sites.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored` — all **16** test binaries pass, 0 failed. Includes the mediator-backed `didcomm_transport_e2e`, which now installs its listener through the production `add_listener` seam rather than reaching past it into the framework's config type — so the new path is exercised end to end against a real mediator.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` — clean (added to my pre-push checks after it caught a broken intra-doc link on #192)

## Next

With the seam in place the swap itself is contained: `start_service`, `add_listener`, `send_message_via`, `spawn_lifecycle_logger` and the dispatcher, all inside `openvtc-core/src/didcomm.rs`. It brings `Delivery::Guaranteed` with it — the framework's `send_message_with_retry` retried on a disconnected listener and `BestEffort` has no retry, so the outbox is the replacement rather than a follow-up. TSP inbound arrives with it too, via `DidCommTransport`'s multiplexed pickup socket.

title: fix(vtc): audit checkpoints honour their own signing key
body:
Closes the limitation recorded when signed audit checkpoints shipped in #708 — partly, and the PR is explicit about where it stops.

## The bug

`verify_checkpoint_state` resolved every `verificationMethod` to the VTC's current signing key:

```rust
verify_checkpoints(&checkpoints, |_vm| Some(public.clone()))
```

The `_vm` says it: the field was **ignored entirely**. Two consequences —

1. A checkpoint naming *some other* key was silently checked against the live one.
2. The per-checkpoint `verificationMethod` that #708 persists **specifically to survive rotation** was decorative.

## The fix, and why it isn't the obvious one

The verifier now honours the field. **The live signer is tried first, for its own method only**; anything else goes to the DID resolver.

That ordering is the whole design, and I got it wrong on the first attempt. Resolving unconditionally looks more correct and **broke every existing checkpoint test** — because it turns a local integrity check into a network operation, dependent on DID resolution being configured and the community's DID being reachable. A deployment with no resolver would have lost checkpoint verification outright. That's an availability regression, and the tests caught it.

Signer-first keeps the overwhelmingly common case — a checkpoint signed by the still-current key — entirely local, and reaches resolution only for a key the signer does not own. Which is exactly the rotated-away case the old code could not handle at all.

An unresolvable key is reported as **its own condition**, not as a bad signature. *"The signing key is no longer published"* is expected after a rotation; *"this checkpoint was forged"* is an incident. The response has to let an operator tell them apart.

## What is still not fixed

Verifying a checkpoint signed under a key **since rotated away** needs the DID document *as it stood at* `checkpointAt`.

Neither `DIDCacheClient::resolve` nor `didwebvh-rs` offers version- or time-addressed resolution — I checked; `didwebvh-rs`'s `version_time` *creates* log entries rather than resolving history. So closing this properly is a **resolver capability**, not something the audit verifier should take on by replaying `did.jsonl` itself. Such checkpoints report `chainBroken` with a detail naming the unresolvable key and the reason.

A deployment whose DID document retains prior verification methods alongside the current one already verifies across rotation today.

The design note's "Known limitation" section is rewritten to say all of this, rather than implying a fix that landed.

## Test

`a_checkpoint_naming_an_unknown_key_is_not_verified_against_the_live_one` — a checkpoint signed by the community's **real** key but naming a different `verificationMethod`. Under the old code it verified, because the named method was never consulted.

## Verification

Full `cargo test -p vtc-service` green (exit 0), 13 in `audit_verify` including the new one. `cargo check --workspace --locked --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check`, clippy — all clean. Version-bump and changelog guards pass.

Refs #708.

title: refactor: move the DIDComm transport module into openvtc-core
body:
Option (1) from #189. **No behaviour change** — this gives the messaging module a testable home *before* the delivery-layer swap rewrites it.

## Why

The module that owns every socket in the TUI had no integration coverage, and the reason was structural: it lived at `openvtc/src/state_handler/didcomm.rs`, and `openvtc` is a **binary-only** crate (`[[bin]]`, no `src/lib.rs`), so no integration test could import it. Its only coverage was two pure unit groups — a regex and an id function.

That is a bad place to start rewriting from. The swap replaces this module's listener construction, dispatch, send and reconnect paths, and its failure mode is `duplicate-channel` plus duelling reconnect loops — which produce neither a compile error nor a failing unit test. They surface as a dropped response on the first burst of requests, in front of a user.

## The move

Nothing in the module referenced the binary crate, so it is mechanical — only `openvtc_core::` → `crate::` prefixes changed.

- `openvtc/src/state_handler/didcomm.rs` → `openvtc-core/src/didcomm.rs`, kept **distinct from `crate::messaging`**, whose module doc promises pure protocol logic with no async I/O orchestration. That purity is what makes the dispatch state machine unit-testable, so transport plumbing must not leak into it. Both module docs now state the split.
- `state_handler` keeps a `pub use openvtc_core::didcomm;` re-export under the old path, so **all nine dependent files' call sites are untouched**. A regression in the messaging layer cannot hide inside an import-churn diff.
- `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` and `tokio-util` promoted from dev-dependencies to dependencies of `openvtc-core`; `regex` added as a dev-dependency for the catch-all tests that came with the module.

The 7 unit tests moved with it — `openvtc` bin 262 → 255, `openvtc-core` lib 257 → 264, total unchanged.

## New coverage, which is the point

`openvtc-core/tests/didcomm_transport_e2e.rs` — two tests that **could not have been written before this move**. Against the real mediator:

1. The production `build_router` routes an OpenVTC protocol type through to the event channel, and the sender and body survive the round trip.
2. An unrelated type reaches **no** handler. The routing gate not leaking was previously only asserted against `Regex::new` — never against an actually-delivered message, which is the claim that matters, since a leak hands unvetted traffic to dispatch.
3. Production `send_message_via` delivers through the mediator.

They use `relationship_listener_config_from_secrets` because it is the one listener builder that takes no `Config`, so the transport path is covered without standing up an encrypted on-disk config. The `Config`-taking builders differ only in where the DID, mediator and secrets come from.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored` — all 16 test binaries pass, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

## Next

The delivery-layer swap of this module, now landing under real integration coverage. As noted on #189 it must bring `Delivery::Guaranteed` with it — the framework's `send_message_with_retry` retried on a disconnected listener and `BestEffort` has no retry, so the outbox is the replacement rather than a follow-up.

title: test(sdk): verify TSP discovery against a deployed VTA (#765 R3.6)
body:
Closes the R3.6 gap on #765.

That issue asked for the `#tsp` extraction to be verified **against a real deployed DID document** rather than the template fixtures alone. It never was — every test in `protocol::matching` and `provision_client::resolve` runs over hand-written JSON — so the discovery leg shipped, merged, and has been live without ever being exercised against a deployment.

## It passes, today, against the deployment named in the issue

```
vta_did      did:webvh:QmWoJD2kpP…:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta
tsp mediator did:webvh:QmTS3a3H9D…:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
didcomm      did:webvh:QmTS3a3H9D…:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
rest_url     None
advertised   [Tsp, Didcomm]
```

## What a real document exercises that a fixture cannot

The deployed VTA advertises its two transports in **different JSON shapes**, both going through the one `ServiceCapabilities` matcher:

```jsonc
{ "id": "…#tsp",         "type": "TSPTransport",
  "serviceEndpoint": "did:webvh:…:mediator" },                 // bare string
{ "id": "…#vta-didcomm", "type": "DIDCommMessaging",
  "serviceEndpoint": [ { "accept": ["didcomm/v2"],
                         "uri": "did:webvh:…:mediator" } ] }   // array of objects
```

**`rest_url == None` is the assertion that pins the actual defect.** This VTA advertises no `#vta-rest`, so before the fix it fell through both extractions and returned a REST URL *synthesized from the DID's own domain* — an endpoint that need not exist, for a node shape this SDK ships templates to mint.

## One deliberate choice

Both transports happen to point at the same mediator here. That is asserted as an **observation and labelled as one** — #765 is explicit that the TSP mediator must be read from the `#tsp` entry rather than assumed equal to the DIDComm one, and a test that quietly relied on them matching would encode exactly the opposite of the requirement.

## Scope

- `#[ignore]`d — resolves a `did:webvh` over the network, so it stays out of the ordinary suite. Verified inert: `0 passed; 2 ignored` on a normal run, and `cfg`-gated on `session` + `provision-client` so it compiles out entirely without them.
- Target overridable via `VTA_LIVE_TSP_DID`, so this does not decay into a test that only proves one host was up.
- Test-only, so no version bump — the guard excludes `tests/` from "source".

```sh
cargo test -p vta-sdk --features session,provision-client,tsp \
    --test tsp_discovery_live -- --ignored --nocapture
```

## Still open

The **correlated round-trip** — `connect_tsp` → `TspSession::request` → reply. That needs a client DID holding an ACL grant on the target VTA, which this test cannot provision. Discovery is the half verifiable without credentials; the transacting half still wants a live exercise before anything delivery-critical rides on it.

Refs #765.

title: test: move the integration harness onto the delivery layer
body:
First step of #189 (adopting `affinidi-messaging-delivery`). Harness only — **no production code changes**.

## Why the harness goes first

The e2e tests build their **own** messaging stack: `common::start_profile_service` constructed a `DIDCommService` with its own `Router` and listeners. So migrating `openvtc`'s production `didcomm.rs` would have left `join_lifecycle_e2e` and `relationship_e2e` passing while exercising the framework being replaced — six green tests, over a real mediator, proving nothing about the change. That is the most convincing kind of false confidence available, so it seemed worth eliminating before rewriting 775 lines on top of it.

Moving the harness first inverts it: these tests become the regression net for the production swap, and the whole pattern is proven end-to-end against a real mediator first.

## What the harness now builds, per profile

- Secrets seeded **before** `ATM::new`, profile via `ATMProfile::from_tdk_profile`, then `profile_add(_, true)` to bring the websocket up — `DidCommTransport::new` fails on a profile with no websocket running.
- `MessagingService::empty` + `add_transport` keyed by the profile's **DID**, not `new`'s `"default"`. The transport *is* the identity here, so the harness exercises the same one-transport-per-identity shape production will.
- `drain_loop_via` on that same id, so a `Guaranteed` send retries over its own socket rather than another identity's.
- Own type-filtered dispatch off `subscribe()`, replacing `Router`/`handler_fn` — the delivery layer has no type-routed dispatch. Same move `vtc-service` made when it cut over.

## Two decisions worth flagging

**Sends use `Delivery::Guaranteed`, not `BestEffort`.** The call being replaced (`send_message_with_retry`) retried on a disconnected listener; `BestEffort` has no retry, so a straight swap would quietly trade a retry for a flake. The outbox *is* that retry. This is also why PR 2's outbox work can't be cleanly deferred out of the production swap — noted on #189.

**Outbound is now two steps.** `MessageTransport::send` takes already-packed bytes (packing is `MessagingProtocol`'s concern, not the transport's), so `ProfileMessaging::send` packs authcrypt via `atm.pack_encrypted` then `send_via`. The framework hid this.

`wait_connected` is polled off `transport_state` — the live connection signal rather than a boot-time latch (R6.2).

The old `start_profile_service` is **deleted** rather than left alongside: two harness paths is how a test silently drifts back onto the retired framework.

## Verification

- All **13** `openvtc-core` test binaries pass with `--include-ignored` — including the mediator-backed `join_lifecycle_e2e` (3) and `relationship_e2e` (3), which now round-trip real DIDComm over the delivery layer
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

The mediator-backed tests went 1.03s → ~2.1s, which is the drain interval plus outbox round-trip. Acceptable for what they now cover.

## Not in this PR

The production swap (`openvtc/src/state_handler/didcomm.rs` and its 8 dependent files). Two things I found while scoping it, both recorded on #189:

- `DidCommTransport::inbound()` **does** stay alive across websocket reconnects, so no restart policy needs reimplementing for receive. But a full ATM task teardown leaves the transport stale where the framework's `RestartPolicy` would have rebuilt it — that gap is mine to handle, and `transport_state` is the signal for it.
- `DidCommTransport` (with its `tsp` feature) already surfaces inbound **TSP** frames off the same multiplexed pickup socket, tagged `Protocol::TSP`. So TSP receive arrives with this migration, without the second socket that blocks #185 item 2b.

title: fix: follow the VTC Trust Tasks onto the spec/vtc registry authority
body:
Follows the VTC Trust Task migration. `vta-sdk` **0.20.0 → 0.20.1** (and `trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.26 → 0.2.38).

The VTC's Trust Tasks have moved off the non-conformant `trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/…` authority onto the canonical registry at `trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/…` — see [verifiable-trust-infrastructure#806](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/806) and [dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#144](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/144).

## Why this is only a lockfile change

The join ceremony and the reciprocal-VMC exchange dispatch on `vta_sdk::protocols` **constants**, not string literals. So the new URIs arrive with the bump:

| Constant | Now reads |
|---|---|
| `MEMBER_REQUEST_VMC_TYPE` | `spec/vtc/members/request-vmc/0.1` |
| `MEMBER_VMC_TYPE` | `spec/vtc/members/vmc/0.1` |
| `JOIN_REQUEST_SUBMIT_RECEIPT_TYPE` | `spec/vtc/join-requests/submit-receipt/0.1` |
| self-remove receipt | `spec/vtc/members/self-remove-receipt/0.1` |

That indirection is exactly why this isn't an audit of every dispatch site.

## The inbound router was already ready

`OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` gained its `https://trusttasks\.org/spec/vtc/.*` arm ahead of the migration — deliberately, since that pattern decides whether a message reaches the handler *at all*, so accepting the new prefix late would have meant migrated traffic silently dropped before dispatch. Good call by whoever landed it; it means this bump carries no routing risk.

It stays **dual-arm** for now. The `openvtc/vtc/` arm retires once no supported VTC emits it, and eight VTC tasks are still on the old authority awaiting a canonical fold.

## Verification

`cargo check --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check` — all clean. Full test suite green (262 + 257 + 26 + the rest, 0 failures).

title: feat(vtc): move VTC Trust Tasks onto the spec/vtc registry authority
body:
The registry now publishes every VTC task ([dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#144](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/144), `trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.38), so the bindings move off the non-conformant `trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/...` authority they were never entitled to use (SPEC 6.1 / 6.5).

**20 old URIs → 22 authored `spec/vtc/<slug>/0.1` slugs.** 22 because two collapsed mounts split.

## All four binding sites, in one change

They cannot lag each other:

| Site | What |
|---|---|
| `vtc-service/src/routes/mod.rs` | the mounts |
| `vta-sdk/src/protocols/` | 4 DIDComm constants with no REST mount |
| `vtc-service/admin-ui/src/` | TypeScript `Trust-Task` header literals |
| `cnm-cli/src/` | CLI |

The SPA is compiled into the binary by `build.rs`, so a partial migration would ship a UI calling URIs the router no longer binds.

## Two mounts split per method

`admin/invites/manage` served **list and create**; `invitations/issue` served **issue and list**. One URI cannot state two contracts, and the exposure differs sharply — issuing returns a bearer credential, listing must never re-disclose one. `task_routes` layers the method router and axum merges same-path method routers per method, so each verb enforces its own task (pinned by `per_method_tasks_on_one_path_are_enforced_independently`).

The SPA's `listInvitations` literally carried the comment *"Reuses the issue Trust Task"*. It has its own now. The test file had `ISSUE_TASK` and `LIST_TASK` set to the same string; they differ now.

## The reciprocal-VMC exchange became three tasks

`members/request-vmc` (admin → VTC) and `spec/members/request-vmc` (VTC → member) would have **collided on one slug** once the parsing-artefact `spec/` segment was dropped. Now `vtc/members/solicit-vmc`, `vtc/members/request-vmc`, `vtc/members/vmc`.

## BREAKING (wire): VTC backup payloads are camelCase

Six types — `ExportRequest`, `ImportRequest`, `BackupEnvelope`, `KdfParams`, `EncryptionParams`, `ImportResult` — carried **no `serde(rename_all)`** and were snake_case, against R3.1 and against every other VTC payload.

`cnm-cli` is fixed on **both** sides: it was sending `include_audit` *and* reading `source_did` / `includes_audit` / `created_at`, all of which would have silently returned `None` against the new server rather than erroring.

**The VTA's backup wire is untouched** — `vta-sdk::client::backup` targets a different service ("Export VTA state") and stays snake_case. Worth checking on review; the two look identical at a glance.

## De-listed, not migrated

`website/deploy` and `website/files/show` are raw-byte operations — a JSON Trust-Task payload cannot carry file bytes — so the registry deliberately has no spec for them. **Removed** from the manifest rather than retired, because `supersededBy` is mandatory on a retired entry and nothing supersedes them. Recorded in `UNPUBLISHED_OK` with that reason.

## The census now reads every binding site

A router-only scan is exactly what produced the wrong residual count corrected in #802 — four tasks are `vta-sdk` DIDComm constants the router never mentions. Two new guards:

- **`no_new_bindings_on_the_retired_authority`** — nothing may bind `openvtc/vtc/` outside a shrinking, reasoned allowlist of the 10 tasks still awaiting a canonical fold. The authority is retired; this stops the migration regressing one literal at a time.
- **`every_bound_vtc_task_exists_in_the_registry`** — every bound `spec/vtc/` URI must resolve through `trust_tasks_rs::schema_index::schema_for`. Cross-checked against the *published registry crate* rather than a hand-maintained list, so a typo or an unauthored slug fails here instead of at runtime.

Also updates `vti-common`'s Trust-Task doc examples and test fixtures off the retired authority. Not bindings — the census deliberately excludes them — but a doc comment demonstrating `openvtc/vtc/...` teaches the shape this change removes.

## ⚠️ Downstream: openvtc must land in the same release

`openvtc` consumes the changed `vta-sdk` constants **and** has a DIDComm regex allowlist that will actively **reject** the new URIs until it upgrades. This is not a soft break.

## Deferred

The 8 tasks that fold onto *canonical* specs rather than `spec/vtc/*`, tracked in `AWAITING_CANONICAL_FOLD` with a reason each. Three are blocked on upstream registry work (`auth/passkey/list`, `config/{export,import}`); three need the delegated `confirm/1.0` gate.

## Verification

`cargo test --workspace` exit 0. `cargo check --workspace --locked --all-targets` clean — the lockfile is in the same commit as the version bumps this time, which is the check that failed on #796. `cargo fmt --check` and clippy clean. All four repo guards pass: version-bumps, changelogs, lockfile self-pins, and the 7-test census.

Refs #710, refs #709.

title: fix: name the community in the persona profile label, not its DID
body:
Follow-up to #183 — the two sibling call sites noted at the bottom of #186, which you asked me to fix with agent-name resolution.

## The defect

The fallback persona-profile label (used when a membership has no `display_name` resolved from the VTC document) ran the VTC DID through `context_path::render_for_display`:

```rust
c.display_name.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| {
    crate::config::context_path::render_for_display(&c.vtc_did).to_string()
})
```

`render_for_display` is a **sub-context** helper — it splits on the last `/` and returns the tail, which is right for `openvtc-glenn/qmxi1pzd4nev` and a no-op on a DID, since a DID has no `/`. So the "slug" fallback was the whole `did:webvh:Qm…` string, and a persona's messaging profile was named after an identifier rather than a party.

Same defect class as #183, in a label position rather than an identity key — which is why the fix differs: here shortening is the *goal*, there it would have introduced a collision.

## The fix

The readable label that arm was reaching for is the community's **verified agent name**, already cached for exactly this purpose. Precedence is now:

```
display_name  ->  verified agent name  ->  VTC DID
```

The DID stays as last resort — unpretty, but the only remaining thing that is true.

- **`ProtectedConfig::cached_agent_name`** becomes the single definition of "the verified name we hold for this DID". `Config::agent_name_for` delegates to it; the loading path needs the lookup before a `Config` exists.
- **`membership_profile_label`** replaces two independent copies of the same expression (`config/mod.rs:433` and `config/loading.rs:302`). The startup and runtime labels have to agree — otherwise a persona's profile is named one thing at launch and another at runtime — and holding one copy makes that structural rather than a comment asking the next editor to remember. The existing comment at the loading site ("matches the runtime listener label") was precisely that comment.

## Only verified names reach the label

Both lookups read the cache of *completed round-trips* and collapse a cached negative to `None`. An unverified `alsoKnownAs` claim cannot reach a label through this path — per `CLAUDE.md`, anyone can claim `bigbank.com/@support` in their own document. The helper's doc states the requirement for future callers, and `an_unverified_community_falls_back_to_the_did` pins it.

## Note on the closure signature

`agent_name` returns an owned `String` rather than a borrow. The two callers hold the cache behind different owners — a `&Config`, and during loading a `ProtectedConfig` later moved into one — and a borrowed return has no lifetime satisfying both (it infers `'static` and the loading-path borrow then outlives the coroutine). The allocation is on the fallback path only, where a label is being built anyway.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` — all green, 0 failed (262 + 257 + …)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

Four new tests: display name wins; verified agent name is used and the *VTC DID* is what gets looked up; an unverified community falls back to the DID; no membership keeps the generic `Persona`.

title: feat(vtc): the remaining 22 VTC tasks — completes the VTC registry surface
body:
Completes the VTC surface in the registry: **every task `vtc-service` binds now has a spec here.** This is what unblocks OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#710, and #709 with it — that issue turns out to be a strict subset, with 19 of its 20 entries moving URI as part of this and the twentieth being a mount-collapse alias rather than a task.

Phase 4a authored 40 VTC tasks; this is the remaining 22.

## What's here

| Family | Tasks |
|---|---|
| `vtc/backup/*` | `export`, `import` |
| `vtc/admin/invites/*` | `list`, `create`, `revoke` |
| `vtc/invitations/*` | `issue`, `list`, `revoke` |
| `vtc/members/*` | `solicit-vmc`, `request-vmc`, `vmc`, `purge`, `removed`, `self-remove-receipt` |
| `vtc/auth/*` | `admin-session`, `recognise/challenge` |
| others | `ceremonies/list`, `directory/query`, `recognition/check`, `relationships/graph`, `policies/test`, `join-requests/submit-receipt` |

Plus three additions to `vtc/_shared/0.1` — `backup`, `invite`, `invitation` — for types two tasks in a family both need. A `$ref` across task boundaries does not resolve under per-file `$id` and the build only *warns*, so shared types have to live there to be real.

## Two structural decisions

**Two mounts were serving several operations under one URI**, distinguished only by HTTP verb: `admin/invites/manage` (list + create) and `invitations/issue` (issue + list). Both are split per method. "Enumerate the registry" and "mint a bearer credential" are different contracts with very different exposure — one URI could not honestly state both, and per-method Trust Tasks are already independently enforced.

**The reciprocal-VMC exchange is three tasks, not two.** The old `members/request-vmc` (admin → VTC) and `spec/members/request-vmc` (VTC → member) would have collided on one slug once the parsing-artefact `spec/` segment was dropped. They are different party pairs with different payloads, so: `solicit-vmc` (admin → VTC), `request-vmc` (VTC → member), `vmc` (member → VTC, with a `#response` receipt).

## Contracts made normative

Several specs write down what the implementation only did by habit — in each case where getting it wrong fails *silently*:

- **`directory/query`** — a withheld field MUST be **absent**, not present-and-null; a subject with nothing visible MUST be `notFound`, not an empty projection. Either alternative turns the directory into a membership oracle: one confirms a field exists while refusing it, the other distinguishes "no such member" from "nothing visible to you".
- **`recognition/check`** — `registryConfigured` is reported alongside `recognised`, because with no registry wired up `recognised: false` means *cannot say*, not *no*. Collapsing them lets a misconfiguration read as a deliberate refusal.
- **`members/solicit-vmc`** — `requested: true` means **dispatched**, not delivered or answered.
- **`invitations/revoke`** — keeps the `newlyRevoked` discriminator and returns the **original** `revokedAt` on a repeat call, so the audit record keeps naming when access was actually withdrawn.
- **`policies/test`** — `result` is returned uninterpreted; a compile error is `evaluationFailed`, not an empty result a caller would read as a deny.
- **`join-requests/submit-receipt`** — sent only after the request is durably recorded. A receipt issued on parse hands the applicant an id for a request that may still be lost.
- **`members/purge`** — super-admin, and the `lastAdministrator` guard has no force flag: a community with no admin cannot grant one, so the operation would be unrecoverable from inside.

## Release housekeeping

Per `CLAUDE.md`: `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`, `npm run build-ts-bindings`, both libraries **0.2.37 → 0.2.38** with a `trust-tasks-rs` CHANGELOG entry, `Cargo.lock` refreshed.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 241 specs, 44 shared schemas, **zero warnings**
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` — green
- **`cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate` — 490 passed.** The run that proves every `payload.invalid-examples.json` entry is genuinely rejected rather than being a placeholder that happens to parse.
- `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs`, `tsc -p tsconfig.json` — clean

Commits are one per family so the history stays bisectable.

body:
feat(vtc): the remaining 22 VTC tasks — completes the VTC registry surface (#144)

* feat(vtc): backup + admin-invites 0.1 (5 of 22 residual tasks)

Authors the first two families of the vtc-service Trust Task residual
(OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#710):

- vtc/backup/{export,import} — encrypted full-state envelope, two-phase
  import (preview by default). BackupEnvelope extracted to
  vtc/_shared/0.1/backup.schema.json: both tasks need it, and a cross-task
  $ref does not resolve under per-file $id.
- vtc/admin/invites/{list,create,revoke} — the former admin/invites/manage
  mount split per method. One URI covering both "enumerate" and "mint a
  credential-bearing URL" is two contracts; per-method Trust Tasks are
  independently enforced. InviteSummary in vtc/_shared/0.1/invite.schema.json.

All payloads camelCase. The VTC's current backup wire types carry no
serde rename_all and are snake_case on the wire — the repointing change
must add it.

npm run validate: 224 specs, 43 shared schemas, zero warnings.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(vtc): invitations 0.1 — the second split mount (8 of 22)

vtc/invitations/{issue,list,revoke}. The former invitations/issue mount
served both issuance and listing under one URI, distinguished only by HTTP
verb — two contracts with very different exposure (issue returns a bearer
credential; list must never re-disclose one). Split per method.

revoke keeps VTC's `newlyRevoked` discriminator, which is the good pattern:
it lets a caller tell "I revoked it" from "it was already revoked", and the
response returns the ORIGINAL revokedAt on a repeat call so the audit record
keeps naming when access was actually withdrawn. Noted in Conformance
because collapsing either would be an easy and lossy simplification.

InvitationSummary in vtc/_shared/0.1/invitation.schema.json, deliberately
carrying no credential material.

These five wire types are already camelCase, so the repointing change is a
URI move only — unlike the backup family in the previous commit, whose types
carry no serde rename_all and are snake_case on the wire.

npm run validate: 227 specs, 44 shared schemas, zero warnings.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(vtc): the reciprocal-VMC exchange, as three tasks (11 of 22)

Membership is reciprocal — the community issues the member a credential and
the member issues one back naming the community. Soliciting that second half
involves three distinct party pairs, and the old URIs collapsed two of them:
`members/request-vmc` (admin -> VTC) and `spec/members/request-vmc`
(VTC -> member) would both have landed on the slug vtc/members/request-vmc
once the parsing-artifact `spec/` segment is dropped.

Split by party pair, slugs confirmed with Glenn:

- vtc/members/solicit-vmc  admin -> VTC. Dispatches the request, returns a
  threadId. `requested: true` claims only that the request was SENT — not
  delivered, not answered. Stated explicitly so this does not become another
  "an Ok means delivered" reading.
- vtc/members/request-vmc  VTC -> member. Proof REQUIRED: communityDid is the
  subject the member is being asked to attest to, so an unauthenticated
  request invites issuing a credential to an impostor. Answering is
  discretionary; silence is not refusal.
- vtc/members/vmc          member -> VTC, plus the #response receipt. Binds
  the credential to the proven sender and rejects a credentialSubject.id that
  is not this community. actsAsSubject: true — the member acts on their own
  membership, which is why it needs no admin capability.

All three wire types are already camelCase; repointing is a URI move.

npm run validate: 230 specs, zero warnings.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(vtc): members purge/removed/self-remove-receipt 0.1 (14 of 22)

- vtc/members/purge — super-admin, not admin. Removal is reversible in
  effect; erasure is not, so it sits a capability above the removal tasks.
  The lastAdministrator guard has no force flag on purpose: a community with
  no admin cannot grant one, so the operation would be unrecoverable from
  inside. A destructive op with an override is one that will be overridden.
- vtc/members/removed — the tombstones purge erases. Purged DIDs MUST NOT
  appear, or the listing defeats the erasure. Discloses the statusListIndex
  mapping, which is the community-internal half of a deliberately public list.
- vtc/members/self-remove-receipt — the community's async acknowledgement
  that a departure actually happened. Proof REQUIRED, not RECOMMENDED: the
  receipt is the member's only evidence their erasure was honoured, and a
  forged one would convince them of a removal that never occurred. Sent after
  the removal takes effect, not on accepting the request.

All wire types already camelCase; repointing is a URI move.

npm run validate: 233 specs, zero warnings.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(vtc): the last 8 tasks, regenerated bindings, 0.2.38 (22 of 22)

Completes the VTC surface in the registry. Every task vtc-service binds now
has a spec here, which is what unblocks
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#710 (and #709, which is a strict
subset of it).

This commit adds vtc/auth/{admin-session,recognise/challenge},
vtc/ceremonies/list, vtc/directory/query, vtc/recognition/check,

title: fix: name the community in the persona profile label, not its DID (#188)
body:
fix: name the community in the persona profile label, not its DID (#188)

The fallback persona-profile label -- used when a membership has no
display_name resolved from the VTC document -- ran the VTC DID through
context_path::render_for_display:

    c.display_name.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| {
        crate::config::context_path::render_for_display(&c.vtc_did).to_string()
    })

render_for_display is a sub-context helper: it splits on the last '/' and
returns the tail, which is right for openvtc-glenn/qmxi1pzd4nev and a
no-op on a DID, since a DID contains no '/'. So the 'slug' fallback was
the whole did:webvh:Qm... string, and a persona's messaging profile was
named after an identifier rather than a party.

Same defect class as #183, in a label position rather than an identity
key. Found while fixing that one.

The readable label that arm was reaching for is the community's verified
agent name, which is already cached for exactly this purpose. Only
verified names are used: both lookups read the cache of completed
round-trips and collapse a cached negative to None, so an unverified
alsoKnownAs claim can never reach a label -- anyone can claim
bigbank.com/@support in their own document.

  * ProtectedConfig::cached_agent_name is the single definition of
    'the verified name we hold for this DID'. Config::agent_name_for
    delegates to it; the loading path needs it before a Config exists.
  * membership_profile_label replaces two independent copies of the same
    expression (config/mod.rs and config/loading.rs). The startup and
    runtime labels must agree or a persona's profile is named one thing
    at launch and another later; one copy makes that structural rather
    than a comment asking the next editor to remember.
  * Precedence is display_name -> verified agent name -> VTC DID. The DID
    remains the last resort: unpretty, but the only thing left that is
    true.

Follow-up to #183 (the sibling call sites noted in #186).
